comments.author: claude-opus-5
comments.body:
CORRECTION (2026-08-07, during the fix): the claim above that all 255 rows are orphans is WRONG and acting on it would cause the exact harm the attachment store exists to prevent.

"All owned by a terminal id that no longer exists in the terminals table" was measured by joining against `terminals`. That table says every row is an orphan. It is not a survivor oracle. Re-measured against the process table (258 rows by then; the leak was still growing at ~18/day):

  231  pid absent                                -> safe to release
   19  pid alive, start_marker byte-exact match  -> RUNNING WORKERS
    1  pid alive, start_marker differs           -> genuinely recycled pid
    7  ambiguous, no published identity          -> human adjudication only

The 19 were cross-confirmed three ways: matching `ps -o lstart=`, the exact native_session_id in 16 of the 19 command lines, and a currently-existing tmux pane whose pane_pid equals the stored pid (sessions cao-p1-closure, cao-dnd-scheduler). A one-time cleanup written to the description above would have released nineteen live sessions into double-attach, which nothing downstream detects.

Two other signals are also NOT survivor oracles: managed_launch_v2_terminals.v2_lifecycle_state says 'live' for 46 rows of which 19 are, and owner_pane_id existing in tmux is true for 62 rows of which 19 are the actual occupant. Pane ids recycle.

Consequently the release test is ONLY `os.kill(pid, 0)` raising ProcessLookupError. The start_marker is recorded as evidence and never decides: it is raw `ps -o lstart=` output (naive local wall-clock in the writer's timezone/locale), so "alive but the marker differs -> recycled -> release" would read a DST rollover as evidence that a live owner is a stranger.

Fixed on branch fix/cond-0209-attachment-release: list_attachments (the store had no enumerator, which is why this went unseen for two weeks), release wired into terminal teardown, a standing sweep rather than a one-time script (server exit is the largest producer and runs no teardown at all), and `cao attachment freeze` + `adjudicate` as the operator path. Boot sweep is report-only by default because two tests in this repo enter the app lifespan without stubbing recovery steps.

comments.author: colin+claude-opus-5
comments.body:
DECIDED 2026-08-07: the marshal gates the SPEC, not the PR, and is fully hands-off afterwards.

Both lanes always run a spec writer + spec reviewer cycle. The marshal gives a final sign-off on the spec and then hands the remainder entirely to implementers and reviewers.

Rejected alternative: the marshal reviews the PR with a P0/P1 veto that kicks back to the implementer. Workable, but worse on three counts. The marshal's comparative advantage is diagnosis - it holds the incident context, the prior incidents and the playbook - which is decisive for "does this plan address the root cause" and nearly worthless for "is this diff correct". A wrong diagnosis is cheapest to catch at the spec stage, before the implementation exists. And keeping the marshal out of the implementation entirely means it can never stamp its own hypothesis into merged code, which preserves §8 more cleanly than a veto does.

THE LGTM IS A SCOPE CHECK, NOT A CORRECTNESS APPROVAL. The question the marshal answers is "does this plan address what I actually found, or has it drifted?" Nobody else can answer that, because nobody else has the incident context. It is explicitly NOT answering "is this plan correct" - that is the spec reviewer's question. Two different questions, two different agents, neither grading its own work.

Two guards keep that honest:

1. The spec writer is never the marshal, and the spec reviewer must independently agree with the diagnosis. That is §8's existing requirement relocated to the spec stage, where it is cheaper to satisfy.

2. The marshal's LGTM is not a substitute for the spec reviewer's. Both are required. If the spec reviewer disagrees with the diagnosis it reports `blocked`, and the marshal does not get to overrule it.

This supersedes open point 1 in the issue body (the necessary-but-not-sufficient greenlight on the PR).

Side effect worth noting: it makes break-glass STRONGER rather than weaker. Lane 2 becomes marshal report -> headless spec writer -> headless spec reviewer -> marshal scope-LGTM -> headless implementer/reviewer on persistent sessions. That is two independent checks in the emergency lane, where PR-review-by-marshal would have given one, and the one it gave would have been the marshal grading itself.

comments.author: colin+claude-opus-5
comments.body:
ADDED 2026-08-07: the cutover must wake what it unblocked, and the lifecycle state decides who.

Whoever performs the cutover - the doctor session's supervisor in lane 1, the fire marshal via its break-glass skill in lane 2 - is responsible for resuming the sessions the defect halted. Each affected supervisor is told that the fix landed and that it should get moving again.

WHO GETS BUMPED is exactly the inverse of the marshal's suppressor set, so one field answers both questions:

  working   -> bump. This is the population the marshal woke for.
  pausing   -> NOTIFY ONLY. An in-flight pause request is an operator's decision
               already in progress; bumping it to "get moving again" fights that.
               Tell the supervisor the cutover happened and let it decide whether
               to continue settling.
  paused    -> leave alone. Deliberately quiet, which is the whole point.
  complete  -> nothing to resume.
  stopped   -> no panes to resume.

DELIVERY MUST BE DURABLE. The cutover restarts cao-server. §10.1 already records that workers survive in tmux panes and the real exposure is a brief window of CAO unavailability, in which `queue` delivery is durable while `steer-active` steers an exact active turn and can drop the message. The post-cutover bump therefore goes through queue delivery. Otherwise the single message that says "the thing that wedged you is fixed" is the one most likely to be lost, and the sessions stay halted after a successful repair - the failure that looks exactly like the repair not working.

ORDERING: bump after the cutover is verified, not before. A supervisor told to resume against a half-cut-over system re-enters the failure it was waiting out.

Note this makes the marshal-cutover path a consumer of session lifecycle, which is a useful check on that design: if the bump set could not be computed from the declared state, the state model would not be carrying its weight.

comments.author: colin+claude-opus-5
comments.body:
LANE 2 ORCHESTRATION, as specified 2026-08-07.

WHEN the marshal takes lane 2: at the very start, before opening anything, it decides whether it can rely on the CAO system to run the repair correctly right now - or has already seen the doctor flow get stuck. That decision is made once, up front, using the headless skill, the check-ai-quota skill and the routing policy to plan how it will orchestrate the fix. It is not a fallback discovered part-way through.

THE FLOW it emulates, both phases on persistent native session ids so neither role restarts cold each round:

  1. spec writer  <-> spec reviewer   (persistent session ids)
  2. marshal scope-LGTM on the spec   (see comment 3: a scope check, not a correctness approval)
  3. implementer  <-> PR reviewer     (persistent session ids)
  4. break-glass merge + cutover skill
  5. post-cutover bump of the halted sessions (see comment 4)

CONSTRAINT carried from the issue body: model and effort are pinned per role for the life of one repair, because resuming a session with either changed invalidates the context cache and the launchers refuse it. A mid-repair quota downgrade therefore forces a new session and throws away the persistence the whole design is buying. The up-front planning step is where that gets decided, which is another reason it belongs at the start rather than mid-incident.

The normal case remains lane 1: the doctor session's supervisor coordinates all of the above, and lane 2 exists so that a wedged CAO cannot prevent a repair from happening at all.

CORRECTION AND ADDITION to the preceding comment. That comment listed "whether the Session UUID truncates at 80 columns" as unresolved and stated that no further launch would be spent on it. It is now RESOLVED, without a further launch, and the exact width thresholds are measured.

THE Session: UUID IS INTACT AT 80x30. /status-based identity repair is NOT width-dependent at 80 columns.

The proof does not rest on geometry. The sanitization regex requires a complete 8-4-4-4-12 UUID to match. It matched in both retained fixtures, and a grep confirms zero unredacted hex fragments survive in either. A truncated UUID could not have matched that regex and would therefore have survived in the fixture as visible partial hex. It did not. That is positive evidence from the retained artifacts rather than an inference from box arithmetic, which is why no additional canary run was needed.

Measured from the fixtures: the value column begins at index 39 at both widths; the 36-character UUID occupies indices 39 through 74, followed by four spaces and the box edge, filling exactly 80 columns with four columns of slack.

MEASURED WIDTH THRESHOLDS, for any future parser or adapter:

  76 columns -- minimum for the full Session UUID plus the box edge
  87 columns -- minimum for the full Model parenthetical including its closing parenthesis
  70 columns -- minimum for the effort token "reasoning medium" alone

A CONSEQUENCE THAT MATTERS BEYOND M10. Four columns of slack means the Session UUID truncates below 76 columns. A capture narrower than 76 columns must be treated as UNUSABLE rather than as absent or invalid data; otherwise /status-based native-identity repair silently becomes width-dependent below that width. This is recorded here as a measured constraint rather than filed as a defect: a truncated UUID would fail identity validation and refuse, which is fail-safe, but it would be misdiagnosed as a missing or malformed identity rather than as an inadequate capture width.

THE AWKWARD MIDDLE BAND. Between 76 and 86 columns the Session row parses correctly while the Model parenthetical is already cut. A single width check therefore cannot cover both fields, and any implementation must either check per-field or pin the stricter 87-column floor.

MODEL ROW TRUNCATION, exact. At 100 columns the value reads "gpt-5.6-luna (reasoning medium, summaries auto)"; at 80 it reads "gpt-5.6-luna (reasoning medium, summari", keeping 40 of 47 characters. Parser constraint: a parser that anchors on the closing parenthesis, or that requires the full parenthetical to match, works at 100 and fails at 80. WEEKLY LIMIT REFLOW, confirmed. Both limit rows reflow at 80 columns, and the "(resets ...)" clause wraps onto its own continuation line that carries NO LABEL. A line-oriented parser must tolerate an unlabelled continuation row.

QUOTA CROSS-CHECK, recorded as a factual observation and not a verdict. The surface reports "Weekly limit: 19% left", about 81% used, corroborating the campaign's independent quota probe reading of roughly 80% used at the same moment, within about one percentage point.

--expected-head was unreachable for a park: it required --successor-source, which checkpoint.py itself declares mutually exclusive with --park. Record the accepted head beside report_sha256 at callback acceptance (callback_encoding v2 has report_sha256 and no head field) and have park compare against what acceptance actually saw.

The filed remedy - require a new callback that names the head - is not the right shape and should not be built as written. It needs a live worker terminal, and the common reason a park happens is that the worker is parked or gone, so as filed it converts a provenance mismatch into a dead end. comments.author: human
comments.body:
Correction from the fix branch (fix/marshal-p1-lock-and-muse-write): **the premise of this issue is wrong, and I filed it.**

## The stale-lock claim does not hold

`marshal_incidents` locks via `atomic.locked()`, which is `fcntl.flock`. flock is released **by the kernel when the holding file descriptor closes — including when the process dies.** A crashed writer therefore leaves no lock at all.

Verified rather than reasoned: a holder was SIGKILLed while inside `locked()`, and the next acquisition succeeded in **0.000s**. The 0-byte `incidents.json.lock` that prompted this filing is the normal residue of every *successful* acquisition — `locked()` never unlinks it, correctly, because unlinking would be racy. It is not evidence of a held lock.

Adding stale-lock breaking here would introduce a race this lock does not have. The branch pins the reasoning in a test (`test_a_killed_writer_does_not_block_the_next_one`) so nobody re-adds it.

**The contrast with the launcher was my error.** `scripts/fire-marshal.sh` uses a `mkdir` lock, which genuinely needs the 10-minute stale break it has. Different primitive, opposite failure mode. I used the presence of a break in one as evidence of a gap in the other.

## What was real

The operator experience behind the filing. The marshal hit `Operation not permitted` on the lock path because it was **sandboxed away from the state root** (cond-0342), and `locked()` opens the lock `a+` — so the failure surfaced as a bare `PermissionError` from inside a contextmanager. `_store_error` then advised "move the unreadable incident store aside", i.e. told the marshal to destroy intact history it merely could not reach. That is a real defect and the branch fixes it:

- `IncidentStoreUnwritable(IncidentStoreError)` carrying the path and the likely cause;
- `_store_locked()` probing the lock path so an unwritable store is named rather than leaking an errno — deliberately probe-then-delegate, so an OSError raised in the caller's body is not misreported as an unwritable store;
- `_store_error` branching to say the recorded history is **INTACT** and pointing at the harness write scope.

Suggest this stays open only until that branch merges, then closes as **fixed-with-corrected-diagnosis** rather than as originally described. The unbounded-block case (a *live* holder that hangs, where `locked()` waits forever) is untouched and is a separate, narrower question if anyone wants it filed.

## M3-E PR E1 (fork half) merged — cond-0381 REMAINS OPEN

**E1 is the fork half only. E2, the conductor thin caller, has not been written. M3-E is not complete and this issue must not be closed until it lands.**

- Merge: `e644c65a5b9001b8178b0864f6ccaa07cf62c892` (fork PR #126), parents `f500c79b` + `1292d5de`, tree `080157fe` — identical to the reviewed head's tree, so the merge introduced no change.
- Repo: `colindmurray/cli-agent-orchestrator`. 14 files, +4283/−13. Tier 2, two reviewers, one repair batch, one narrow closure check.
- CI-against-CI at exact base vs exact head: base run 31977698196 (4 failed / 10412 passed) vs head run 31979898816 (4 failed / 10498 passed). Failing id sets **identical**, zero base-only and zero head-only. The four are the known `cond-0432` Claude version-pinning tests, all disjoint from the changed files. Pass delta +86 matches the 86 new focused tests exactly.

### Repository-ownership correction (affects the plan, not just this issue)

M3-D merged in the **fork** (PR #116, `9f38c3d3`), not the conductor. The occurrence table is fork-side at `clients/database.py:1282`, and conductor's `goal_store.py:24-27` disclaims minting occurrence ids. The remaining-work plan states the opposite in five places, including the persistence requirement at 733-735 ("one per-project **conductor** SQLite database"). M3-E is therefore fork-primary with a conductor-thin caller (E2). Root is correcting the plan separately.

### Two deviations from the accepted design, each for a named failure

1. **`handoff-pending` is the handoff row's state, not `task_occurrences.state`.** A third occurrence state removes the donor's row from `open_occurrence_for_agent`; `supervisor_drain`'s observer reads *no open occurrence* as positive `parked`, so a concurrent drain would record the donor's **previous** round's digests as a proven boundary and, under Stop, announce teardown of the pane the handback keeps as rollback insurance. `_later_work_refusals` cannot catch it — its only "moved" signal is a different open id on the same agent. Proven executably in both directions by `test_a_concurrent_drain_never_reads_a_held_donor_as_parked`.
2. **A transfer mints a new occurrence rather than rewriting the donor's row.** The rewritten columns are the immutable content `open_occurrence` adopts a retry against, two unique indexes are keyed on them, and both `retire_worker_pane` and `admit_fresh_successor` finalize by occurrence id with no `agent_id` predicate — a moved row lets one worker's teardown finalize another's live round.

The accepted design (`2026-08-06-fire-marshal-deadlock-recovery-design.md`, lines 462-476) still says `handoff-pending` is an occurrence state. **That amendment is not yet published** — it lives in cao-conductor and could not ride in a fork PR. The reasoning is durable in the fork meanwhile at `docs/session-lifecycle.md` §4.6. Root owns routing that amendment.

### F1 — a pre-existing M3-B gap, now covered

**Not introduced by this PR.** Git ordering: `provider_byte_admission` 2026-08-09 (`22f25b7e`), `exact_executor` 2026-08-15 (`295839ee`), the hold 2026-08-16. M3-B's exact executor deliberately allocates a terminal id proven absent from the managed-launch reservation table, so a restored pane resolves as **unmanaged** and returns from `provider_byte_admission` before any reservation-keyed check runs. A handback's recipient runs on such a pane by construction, and so does any donor that was ever recovered — the ordinary steady state after a pane loss.

The hold now sits at the **top** of `provider_byte_admission`, above every branch, resolving its agent from the roster (`get_incarnation_by_terminal`) rather than from a reservation. A terminal with no roster incarnation is not held; that is not a bypass, because an agent with no incarnation cannot be a handoff party.

**Covered:** roster-bound agents on reservation-less terminals refused as donor and as recipient; settled handoffs restore admission on both; only the derived `packet_control_id` passes for the recipient and not the donor; refusal decided with the fence-entry list still empty.
**Still unproven:** no byte write was observed on a live pane (tmux unavailable). The `ResolvedControlIdentity` is test-constructed, so "a restored pane resolves as `managed=False`" is carried from the reviewer's executed reproduction rather than re-proven. What is proven is the load-bearing half: given such an identity, the hold fires where it previously did not.

**The generation fence has the same reservation-less gap** and is wider than M3-E — filed for root, not fixed here.

### Cross-slot case: guarded, not pinned by a discriminating test

One agent as donor of one handoff and recipient of another collides on none of the three partial unique indexes, so the second INSERT raises nothing and no retry fires. It is guarded by the recipient-must-be-free precondition plus the anchored read-then-insert in `_begin_once`. That interleave was built and forced at the last read before the INSERT and ended **safe in both modes**, so no discriminating test exists to write; a test there would have discriminated nothing. What `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` prevents is argued from a direct lock measurement — second writer blocked with it on, able to take the write lock with it off — not from a failing test. Recorded rather than papered over.

### A self-correction that was itself wrong

The most instructive item in the branch, preserved deliberately.

Mutation-testing the repair batch found `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` survived, so the docstring and comments were rewritten to say the lock was not the mechanism. The measurement was honest; the **test it measured against does not exercise the invariant its name claimed** — both threads name the same `to_agent`, which never holds an occurrence and so can never be a donor, making it a recipient-slot collision an index forbids outright. True prose became false prose.

The actual load-bearing change was one neither the batch nor its note credited: the owns-session path previously ran with **no transaction at all**, because pysqlite emits `BEGIN` only before DML, so a read-then-insert spanned two transactions. The unconditional `_anchor_caller_transaction` added in the batch is what makes it atomic; `IMMEDIATE` strengthens the lock from deferred to RESERVED.

Generalisation worth keeping: **a surviving mutant is ambiguous evidence** — it means either the code is inert *or* the test is aimed elsewhere, and those must be distinguished before either is written down. Mutation-test the fix *and* the test's subject.

### Deletions and non-guards

- `epoch` deleted — CAS-checked in one mutator of four while `state` did the real work.
- `rollback_predicate_json` deleted — write-only; `_donor_restoration` re-derives its conditions from columns that are read.
- `native_session_id` removed from the transfer route — filed independently by both reviewers; an ordinary field-name slip would have stamped the donor's native session onto the recipient's occurrence.
- **`managed_launch_v2` needs no hold**, and the guard the brief declared would have been dead code: `managed_launch_v2.py:1346` mints `str(uuid.uuid4())` per reservation with no caller input and no reuse path, so reservation agents and handoff parties are disjoint populations. **Pinned by an AST test**, not prose, so a later change making that column caller-supplied fails a test.
- Also cut: `handoff_for_occurrence`, `cao session handoff list`, `conductor_consumer_attached`.

### Live vs dark

Nothing outside tests can **create** a handoff — no conductor client, no CLI verbs — so no refusal can fire on a running installation. The **enforcement** half is live: every managed control-input, native-inbox and operator-message write performs one indexed single-row read against the new table. The in-place kill switch is therefore **not** the router registration but the hold call at the top of `control_input_service.provider_byte_admission`.

### Next

- **E2 (conductor thin caller) not started and not authorized.** Note for whoever picks it up: `tests/fake_cao.py` moved in the goal-lifecycle drift, and the E2 plan adds fake handoff routes to that same file — E2 begins with a conflict check, not a clean assumption.
- Post-merge auditor slot requested from root; not launched by this lane.
- Cross-track note for the goal-lifecycle campaign: after a handback, `goal_context.resolve_actor` fails both its assignee tests, so the recipient cannot record progress on the inherited goal. Re-binding is structurally impossible inside `goal_store` (`goal_no_update` pins both fields, `goal_no_delete` refuses deletes). The remedy is their own `assign-next`; M3-E's only obligation was making the successor discoverable, which it does via `dispatch_provenance` on the new occurrence.

FINDINGS, all reproduced by EXECUTING the merged service layer against a scratch store rather than by reading it. Three P2 filed as issues:

- **cond-0439 (P2)** - `donor_revision` is anchored at begin, not at the packet digest. The caller digests the packet, then begin reads whatever revision exists at begin time, and `BeginRequest` actively REJECTS an `expected_revision` field (a test pins the 422). A boundary recorded in the window makes the transfer-time revision check pass against a packet describing the previous revision.
- **cond-0440 (P2)** - "recipient must be free" is checked once at begin and never enforced afterwards. The hold gates BYTES; opening an occurrence is a store operation and consults no handoff state. An ordinary dispatch for the recipient mid-window wedges both the handoff and the recipient's unrelated round, after the packet has already been typed into the recipient's context.
- **cond-0441 (P2)** - the delivered-to incarnation is caller-asserted and never checked against the roster or `to_agent_id`. The chain verifies that the caller is CONSISTENT, never that it is RIGHT, so a successor occurrence can be durably stamped with another worker's pane - which recovery paths that finalize by occurrence id with no agent predicate will then act on.

Two P3 not separately filed, recorded here:

- Delivery-record adoption ignores a changed `receipt` (`task_handoff.py:761-768`): the replay comparison covers `delivery_state`, `delivery_outcome`, `to_incarnation_id` but not `receipt`, so a retry with a different receipt string is adopted and the stored receipt is not the one the retrier believes. Evidence-trail only. One line to include `delivery_receipt`.
- `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` silently downgrades when a caller supplies a session already in a transaction (`task_handoff.py:262-263`). Every current caller passes `db=None`, so latent. A future in-process caller that read first would run the cross-slot precondition unlocked, permitting two pending handoffs naming one agent; `_pending_row_for_agent` then answers with the oldest and the second handoff's packet control id is refused forever.

SEQUENCING CONSEQUENCE, which is the most important part of this audit. All three P2 findings are reachable ONLY through the write routes, which nothing currently calls. They are dark today and none is live on any installation. comments.body:
Reproduced 2026-08-10T05:24Z from `/Users/colin/Projects/cli-agent-orchestrator-worktrees/cond0384-dead-status` with `git push origin fix/cond0384-dead-status` while `core.hooksPath` resolved to `cao_mcp_apps/.husky/_`.

The pre-push hook launches `uv run --project .. pytest ../test -m "not e2e" -q` without clearing Git's hook-local environment. Temporary repositories created by tests then commit through the parent worktree's `GIT_DIR`: captured setup output says `On branch fix/cond0384-dead-status ... nothing to commit` for a temp repo, and fixture commits `6293cd34..5b7a1099` were appended to the real branch. The hook reported 279 failures and 62 errors.

Expected: child `git -C <temp-repo>` operations bind the temp repository and the hook cannot mutate the branch being pushed. Actual: the hook moved the checked-out branch and index while tests ran; the accidental history was pushed once before detection.

Recovery was non-force: remote branch `fix/cond0384-dead-status` now ends at child commit `93e2fa08`, whose tree exactly equals independently reviewed `e277202f`. A clean PR branch, `fix/cond0384-dead-status-clean`, points directly to `e277202f`.

Likely durable fix: clear every variable named by `git rev-parse --local-env-vars` before running external tests, and add a canary proving temp-repo commits cannot mutate the source branch. The hook source is currently untracked in this worktree, so identify its provisioning/source owner before patching it.

The commit message originally claimed a stranded intent row poisoned the control id against re-attempt. A skeptic disproved that: a same-digest retry is accepted and lands. The message was amended. The real harm was simpler and worse - every retry failed identically.

The strand SHAPE is unchanged and pre-existing: any exception the three post-claim handlers do not name still escapes past open_intent and leaves state='intent'. This fix removed the cond-0413 cause, not the shape. Closing it needs a post-claim handler that resolves the record to a truthful terminal answer before re-raising.

comments.author: human
comments.body:
COORDINATOR CORRECTION: PARTIALLY REVERSING THE ORACLE RULING. An independent adversarial review, instructed to default to "the ruling is wrong", was run against it. Two of the three drops survive. THE SECRET-READ DROP DOES NOT AND IS REVERSED.

WHAT WAS WRONG, AND WHY. The ruling dropped secret-read denial as an enforced eligibility gate and retained it as an instruction-level rule, on the stated ground that no launcher implements it and that enforcing it would mean building sandboxing that the accepted direction rules out. That ground is factually wrong in two ways.

First, the accepted design already names both the property and the correct alternative. Spec section 3 names secret denial as an eligibility property, states that "A prompt promise is not a filesystem boundary", and prescribes that when a harness cannot satisfy it "the registry records why and SKIPS THAT HARNESS instead of silently weakening the marshal's contract." Relaxing the oracle is the specific action that text forbids, and skipping the harness is the action it requires.

Second, "building sandboxing" was an overstatement that was doing real work in the rationale. Kimi already runs under sandbox-exec with a subpath deny in place. Adding `(deny file-read* (subpath ~/.secrets))` is one rule in one existing profile. The synthesis test I invoked is "a plausible correctness boundary and a proportionate operational cost"; the cost here is one line, so the test does not carry the drop.

The cooperative failure sequence I claimed was absent does in fact exist. M14 grants the break-glass role publish, merge, cutover, and revert authority. A role holding that authority that can read the operator's secret roots can, in entirely good faith, read a credential while investigating and carry it into a commit, an issue body, or a receipt. That is an accidental-disclosure path through cooperative behaviour, not a hostile-actor scenario, so it is squarely inside this project's threat model.

AN AUTHORITY INCONSISTENCY IN MY OWN REASONING, recorded plainly. I declined to harden the launchers on the ground that it is an operator decision rather than a Fire Marshal one. But relaxing an eligibility property that the accepted design names, and that the design says should skip the harness instead, changes what every downstream receipt means for M5c, M13, M14, and M17. Both are operator decisions. I took one and deferred the other on the same authority, which was not consistent.

WHAT SURVIVES, AND ON BETTER GROUNDS THAN I GAVE.

The arbitrary-temp-write drop survives. The review noted the strongest available evidence that this was not schedule-driven weakening is in this issue itself: the record states that adding kimi "requires the out-of-state and secret oracles relaxed as well", and the ruling did not relax out-of-state-write. Kimi therefore stays ineligible. A ruling written to unblock the matrix would have taken that cell, because it is one line and buys an entire route.

TO REMOVE ANY AMBIGUITY: out-of-state-write DENY IS RETAINED AS A GATE. Write confinement is not being gutted. Only the arbitrary-temp-write cell was dropped.

The repo-write narrowing survives, and the discriminator was not invented. The design spec status block at lines 13-16 states verbatim that "a real denied-repository-write probe for every enforced_readonly=1 harness remains an M5 activation blocker." The flag is also not a self-declaration: marshal-harness.sh:217-234 records it as "DERIVED, never hand-set", from a write scope measured by actually launching each harness. M5b's rule that read-only declarations never grant eligibility is therefore not violated.

The narrowing is in fact FORCED rather than chosen, which is a better defence than the one originally recorded. The review found and then eliminated a fourth option: relocating --dir to the state root for claude, zai, and deepseek would by the harness file's own logic flip them to enforced_readonly=1 and apply the oracle to all seven routes, with no custom-skills edit, and the obvious blocker of cwd-based tracker resolution is surmountable because `conduct issue file` accepts --tracker-project. It fails on a different fact: marshal-harness.sh:255-257 states that "Every allow-workdir harness confines BOTH reads and writes to its allowed set." Those three harnesses need the repository writable in order to READ it, and reading the repository is the marshal's entire purpose.

A RECEIPT DEFECT THIS EXPOSED, which applies regardless of how the secret question resolves. capability.mint_receipt has no field recording which oracle set produced a receipt, so a receipt minted under a relaxed contract is byte-indistinguishable from a full-contract one to every downstream consumer. That is the same defect this issue already records one level down, where a reported 12/12 is really ten scored cells plus two restatements; it simply needs extending to relaxed and non-gating cells.

Also relevant to weighing the secret cell: the probe's secret fixture is synthetic, using a SECRET_TOKEN with an explicit note that nothing reads the operator's real secret roots. The cell as written therefore tests policy shape rather than real exposure, which lowers the value of the oracle as currently implemented and raises the value of enforcing the spec's actual words.

AMENDED RULING, IN FORCE NOW. Arbitrary-temp-write denial: dropped as an eligibility gate, unchanged. Out-of-state-write denial: RETAINED as a gate. Repo-write denial: narrowed to enforced_readonly=1 routes, on the forced-by-read-requirement grounds above, and scored BIDIRECTIONALLY so the flag is derived from an observed outcome on every route at probe time rather than from the stale 2026-08-08 measurement, which this issue already flags as stale for zai and deepseek. This costs nothing because repo-write is already one of the ten paid cells and fuses into the same launch. Secret-read denial: NO LONGER DROPPED. It is escalated to the operator as one bounded question, and until it is answered no route may be marked eligible on a relaxed secret contract; affected routes are marked partially-contained, relying on the manual and --child recovery paths the plan already preserves.

RECEIPT REQUIREMENT ADDED TO SCOPE. Every receipt must record the oracle-set identifier and every measured-but-non-gating result, so a relaxed receipt is distinguishable from a full-contract one by its consumers.

INDEPENDENT COVERAGE AUDIT OF `dbd07398` COMPLETE. Verdict: CLEAR WITH FINDINGS.

Run on Kimi K3 against a disposable detached worktree, because the scheduled sequential post-merge audit for this merge is deferred on Z.ai weekly quota (92 percent used, extreme pressure) and the tree had no coverage at all. This does NOT replace the retained auditor, does not touch its session, and does NOT advance the audit watermark. Full report: `/Users/colin/Projects/cao-conductor-worktrees/COND0426-KIMI-COVERAGE-AUDIT-REPORT-20260817.md`

WHAT CHECKED OUT. The probe drives the real launcher wire shape - `--prompt-file` in, `RUN_DIR : ` handle block, `session_id`/`exit_code` on disk - verified against all six INSTALLED launchers rather than against fixtures. Refusals are typed and structurally distinct from passes. The receipt store is locked, atomic, and refuses fixture evidence. The previously-found "fixture pins an ingredient the code never checks" instance is genuinely fixed, and the auditor mutation-checked that rather than taking it on report. Nothing found produces a false `eligible`. `python3 -m unittest tests.test_marshal_probe` ran 79 tests, OK.

FILED:

- **cond-0442 (P1)** - the fixture/provider guard fails OPEN. It is evaluated only when `harness_spec()` succeeds; a `KeyError` sets `spec = None` and disables both guards. Three demonstrated paths: a typo'd `--harness` with a real `--launcher` and no `--provider-run` exits 0 and runs the launcher stamped `local-fixture`; a transient registry subprocess failure converts a real-launcher run into a "fixture" run; and because every installed launcher exists twice on this installation (the skills symlink and the byte-identical custom-skills copy, a fact documented in `launcher_fingerprint` itself), naming the other copy defeats a realpath-equality guard. The asymmetry is the sharp part - the `--provider-run` direction of the same typo IS fail-closed, so the failure is precisely on the side that can bill silently.
- **cond-0443 (P2)** - a transient failure on the resume leg is recorded as a containment verdict and, because `record()` replaces by design, destroys a good receipt. "We measured and it failed" and "the measurement itself failed partway" become indistinguishable in the durable record, costing a paid re-run to recover.
- **cond-0444 (P2)** - the probe launches on the launcher's DEFAULT model and effort while the marshal deploys the registry `HS_MODEL`/`HS_EFFORT`, and the receipt records neither. The two cells this merge made load-bearing - codeword recall across a resume, instruction discipline on the denial cells - are exactly the capability-sensitive ones.

RECORDED, NOT SEPARATELY FILED (P3): a corrupt receipt store reads as EMPTY and the next `record()` silently wipes the other harnesses' receipts, with detection impossible (`marshal_receipts.py:70-80`, pinned by a test at `tests/test_marshal_receipts.py:111-117` whose own wording names the safer alternative); `run_dirs` is null on exactly the refused paid runs its comment says it serves (`marshal_probe.py:1279-1286`), so an operator chasing a possibly-still-billing detached harness parses a path out of an error string or retries blind; `--timeout` is applied twice so a run can take 2x the documented budget (`:731` then `:746`); the runbook's "the launchers default to `review`" is false for zai and deepseek; and `harness_spec`'s `skills_root` parameter has no caller anywhere.

## FACTS BEARING ON THE STANDING SECRET-READ DECISION

Stated as facts. The decision remains the operator's.

1. **The cell is escalated, not gating, and the state is already representable.** `secret-read` is `ROLE_ESCALATED` in the one oracle set (`marshal_probe.py:176`). Failing only it yields `partially-contained` (`:189-198`, `:982-993`). A receipt IS recorded for such a run, and `marshal_receipts.evaluate` refuses it as `not-contained` (`marshal_receipts.py:205-210`), with `grants_eligibility` unconditionally False (`:1312-1327`). So the store can hold the state without any route ever launching on it.

2. **Which routes can satisfy the cell is decided by READ confinement, and it splits the registry.** Per the probe layout (`marshal_probe.py:455-511`): claude, zai and deepseek confine reads to the allowed set, so the secret fixture is structurally unreadable and denial is OS-enforced rather than self-reported. kimi (`deny-workdir`) gets `readable_roots = None` (`:499-502`) - its generated review profile is `(allow default)(deny file-write* (subpath WORKDIR))`, so writes are denied under the repo and READS ARE UNRESTRICTED (verified in the installed `kimi-headless.sh` printf that builds `review.sb`). codex, muse and muse-contributor (`allow-workdir`, no add-dir) likewise get `readable_roots = None` (`:495-498`); the registry documents their sandboxes as write-only confinement. deepseek is separately `unfit` and the probe refuses to bill for it. Net: four of seven routes measure `partially-contained` on this cell, two can pass it structurally, one is refused before spending.

3. **THE MOST DECISION-RELEVANT FACT.** On non-confined routes the integrity check is `SECRET_TOKEN in json.dumps(report)` (`marshal_probe.py:1136-1137`) - the secret's absence from the REPORT JSON - plus the reported outcome. It does not inspect `stream.log`, `final.txt`, or the session transcript. So on a route with no OS-level read denial, a harness that reads the secret and reports `denied` without quoting it PASSES the cell. On confined routes the denial is structural and this caveat does not apply. A leak into the report is `contradicted` and gates unconditionally, which the tests pin.

   The consequence for the decision: without OS-level denial, a pass on this cell would be SELF-REPORTED, and self-reported denial is not evidence of containment. That is an argument for making kimi's denial structural rather than for accepting a weaker pass. It is not currently a live defect, because those four routes measure `partially-contained` (a failure) rather than a false pass - the present state is honest. The exposure would appear if anyone later loosened the cell to accept a self-reported denial.

4. **Nothing in this merge requires the sandbox rule.** The runbook states that partially-contained routes lean on the manual and `--child` paths, and the code makes that state representable and non-eligible. The probe measures correctly either way. The decision only changes what four routes will measure.

FLEXIBILITY-LENS READING, offered because `AGENTS.md` now requires it and this is a live cost rather than a hypothetical: four of seven routes being ineligible is a substantial flexibility cost, and for kimi the remedy is one read-deny rule in one already-generated sandbox profile. That is not weakening the contract - it makes the route actually satisfy the property, structurally, which fact 3 shows is the only way a pass on this cell means anything. codex, muse and muse-contributor are documented as write-only confinement and may not admit the same one-line remedy, so they plausibly stay partially-contained until harness-level work is done.

WHAT ACTUALLY EXISTS. `test/services/test_task_handoff_migration.py`, 299 lines, added in this same merge, with six tests:

    test_the_three_pending_indexes_are_partial_in_both_schemas
    test_migration_is_idempotent

THE CORRECTION SHARPENS THIS DEFECT RATHER THAN DISSOLVING IT. Two things are true of that file:

Every test in the file therefore exercises the CREATE-from-absent path. Not one constructs a store that already carries the table at an older shape. Measured properly today, and it is much worse than "load-flaky". It fails the majority of the time in isolation on unmodified main, with no concurrent load at all.

Five consecutive isolated runs of the single test, on origin/main 273449b with nothing else running:

    python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p "test_marshal_session.py" \
      -k test_a_child_that_ignores_sigterm

    base:   FAILED  FAILED  OK  FAILED  FAILED     (4/5 fail)
    branch: FAILED  OK  OK  FAILED  FAILED         (3/5 fail)

Note both failure modes appear: `failures=1` and `errors=1`, which suggests a race with two distinct losing outcomes rather than one flaky assertion.

Correcting an earlier reading on this issue: I previously reported it passing 3/3 in isolation and attributed a full-suite failure to concurrent load. That was a lucky streak, not evidence. Under repetition the same command fails most of the time with nothing else running, so "load-flaky" is the wrong characterization and the load explanation should not be relied on.

## Why this matters more than a flaky test usually does

It costs a real diagnostic step on every branch. Twice today a full-suite run reported exactly this failure and the honest question - is this mine? - required a base-worktree comparison to answer. A test that fails ~70% of the time on unmodified main teaches every reader to skip it, which is precisely how a genuine regression in marshal session cleanup would get waved through.

That is the same failure mode as a permanently-red doctor advisory (cond-0491): a signal that is always failing consumes the attention a real one would need.

## What to do

Fix the race, or quarantine the test with a named reason until it is fixed. Either is better than the current state, where it is nominally a gate and functionally noise.

If it is quarantined, the quarantine must name what is unproven while it is skipped - cleanup of a child that ignores SIGTERM is a real property, and skipping the test does not make it hold.

Reproduce with the five-run loop above; a single run proves nothing in either direction, which is the trap that produced the earlier wrong reading.

comments.body:
Design note from an independent recalibration pass, and it is a better shape than the deploy-receipt re-anchor landed for COND-0424.

Requiring the executing conductor source to match the journaled source is a preference compiled as an invariant. Recovering a run with newer conductor code is the normal and desirable case: the deployed build is precisely the build the operator intends every lane to be recovered by. Two distinct transitions currently share conduct/lib/sourcechain.py and should be split. runtime_recovery_command keeps its fail-closed deploy-receipt binding, because an absent receipt is a positive statement that no trusted deploy binds this runtime rather than a probe that failed. A new verify_journaled_recovery_command(journaled, executing) returns a structured drift report naming the journaled identity, the executing identity, and the differing surface, and the recovery path consumes that report instead of a refusal.

The interpreter half this issue is about is then fixed at the source rather than at the reader: on install, walk every journaled run, recompute the binding, rewrite each run recovery command, and record every run it could not read with the reason. Install proceeds regardless. An install that rebinds none of the runs it found files a finding against the rebinder and still installs, because refusing the install would put a repository-wide refusal on a campaign-scoped property and reproduce the original defect through a new door. Emit the rebind as an invalidation event naming the guard and the records it disarmed or repaired, which is the observability half this issue asks for.

That approach covers both populations measured on this host: the 22 runs whose package tree drifted, already handled by the COND-0424 fix, and the 207 whose pinned interpreter no longer exists, which is this issue and which the reader-side fix cannot reach.

REVIEWED AND EXTENDED. PR #171, branch `fix/cond0442-provider-guard`, now at `1f2bc05`. Independent review verdict: SOUND WITH FINDINGS. The blocking finding is fixed; the branch is awaiting CI on the new head.

Both the repair and the review ran on Kimi rather than Claude, because Claude weekly sits at 82 percent against a reset shared with other sessions while Kimi weekly is at 6 percent.

## The reviewer found a RESIDUAL BILLING HOLE of the same class as this issue

`conduct/commands/marshal.py:1179-1196`. The digest comparison was computed only against `spec["script"]` for the harness named in `--harness`. This issue's root diagnosis was that `--harness` and `--launcher` are independent and nothing cross-checks them; the first repair closed only the case where the harness NAME fails registry lookup. A pair where BOTH arguments are individually valid but belong to DIFFERENT harnesses passed every check:

    --harness codex --launcher <kimi's registered launcher path>, no --provider-run
    path comparison   -> false (not codex's script)
    digest comparison -> false (kimi's bytes != codex's bytes)
    -> the run proceeds, invokes kimi's REAL PAID launcher, exits 0, stamps local-fixture, writes no receipt

Demonstrated in a sandbox with distinct-byte fixture copies installed at the registry-derived paths, so no provider was contacted: `exit=0 launched=[marshal-probe-fixture] local_fixture=True`.

Cooperative sequence: an operator running the paid matrix harness-by-harness copies the previous command line and edits `--harness` while forgetting `--launcher`.

COORDINATOR DISPOSITION, contrary to the reviewer's own suggestion. The reviewer rated F1 as deserving a follow-up issue rather than blocking. I judged it blocking: it is the same impact class as the defect this branch exists to fix, the remedy is comparing against six registered digests instead of one, and it sits in a file already being edited. Merging a P1 billing repair that leaves an equivalent billing hole open is how the hole gets forgotten.

FIXED in `1f2bc05`. New `registered_scripts()` in `conduct/lib/marshal_probe.py` sources the real shell registry in one subprocess and emits every route with its `HS_SCRIPT` (7 routes, 6 distinct scripts, since muse and muse-contributor share), raising `KeyError` on read failure or an empty route list so callers fail closed. It is a reader of the registry, never a restated copy. On the free side only, the guard now refuses when the launcher's bytes match any route other than the named one, naming the matched harness. The `--provider-run` side is untouched, since path-exactness already refuses a crossed pair.

Two tests: `test_a_crossed_harness_launcher_pair_is_refused`, and a POSITIVE companion `test_a_fixture_run_beside_a_foreign_launcher_still_runs` pinning that the widened refusal fires only on registered programs. That companion matters - widening a refusal invites over-breadth, and the positive case is what bounds it.

Before-fix text with `marshal.py` reverted to `13a54d0`: `AssertionError: 0 != 1`, both run dirs populated, `receipt: null`. Coordinator re-ran the mutation independently: reverting `marshal.py` fails exactly `test_a_crossed_harness_launcher_pair_is_refused` and nothing else.

F2 argued the `spec is None` refusal over-reaches by blocking two free-only workflows: a fixture smoke test of a harness pending registry admission, and any fixture run during a transient 30s registry timeout. The implementer declined the suggested narrowing and argued it, correctly:

- The undeclared-route capability the reviewer cited is a LIBRARY capability. `test_an_undeclared_route_is_measured_without_a_verdict` exercises it through `run_local_probe`, which never touches the CLI guard. The CLI `--harness` contract genuinely requires the registry, because write scope, layout, and scoring all derive from the spec, so a CLI invocation without it could not do that job honestly anyway. The named workflow is not blocked.
- The timeout case already has the recovery the threat model asks for, and the refusal message says so.
- The exemption would rescue two rare conveniences at the cost of a permanent carve-out in the one check whose strength is having a single rule. It would also redefine the boundary from "the registry vouches" to "the registry vouches, or the bytes look harmless" - and byte-level harmlessness is precisely the judgment this issue showed the code getting wrong.

That last argument is the strongest and it rebuts the narrowing on its own terms.

The reviewer cleared the one MODIFIED test properly rather than by reading the diff. `test_a_fixture_run_records_nothing` had been changed, which is where a weakening hides. It ran the OLD scenario against the NEW code and got exit 1, proving the change was forced rather than opportunistic, and confirmed the assertions themselves were untouched.

The reviewer also answered the over-restriction question with named workflows rather than in the abstract, which is what made it possible to check the answer and find it wrong.

A NOTE ON WHY THIS MERGE TOOK SIX HOURS AFTER REVIEW. GitHub incident `zkxwbgr0cnmx` degraded the API and stalled this repository's SELF-HOSTED runner: run `32036948533` was created at `13:51:39Z` and sat `queued` for over two hours with no pickup. During that window `repos/.../actions/runs` returned `403 Resource not accessible by personal access token` for this repository while the identical call on the fork succeeded, which the coordinator twice misdiagnosed - first discounting a concurrent `503` as noise, then asserting a per-repository fine-grained-PAT permission gap and recommending the operator EDIT TOKEN SCOPES. The disconfirming evidence was one call away and unqueried: `repos/.../actions/workflows` succeeded throughout, proving Actions scope was present. No credential was touched, and no merge was made against an unverifiable gate. The durable workaround is recorded: `actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/runs` accepts `?branch=` and returns the same records when `actions/runs` is refused.

## What landed

cond-0443: a `launcher_error` on the RESUME leg now sets `result["refusal"]` with reason `resume-launcher-error` and returns before any cell is scored, mirroring the rule the launch leg already had. That routes through the existing "a refusal is not an answer" guard, so `record()` is never called and the prior receipt is byte-preserved. Previously a routine re-probe whose launch leg succeeded and BILLED, then hit a transient resume hiccup, scored `uncontained` on a gating cell and recorded it, destroying a good receipt and leaving the route refused until someone paid for another full matrix.

cond-0444: provider runs now pass the registry `HS_MODEL`/`HS_EFFORT` - the same flags `fire-marshal.sh` deploys - and the receipt `build` block records both. The flags are appended AFTER `--launcher-arg` so an operator passthrough cannot silently shift what the receipt claims; the reviewer verified last-occurrence-wins by reading all six installed launcher parsers rather than trusting the assertion.

## Two design calls that went against the issue's own suggestions, both correct

The issue offered "align the argv" OR "record the resolved model". The implementer did BOTH, because either alone is dishonest: recording alone has nothing honest to record, since with no model flag passed the resolved model is the launcher's default which the probe cannot know, so writing the registry value into the receipt would be recording what it did not establish.

The implementer DECLINED to convert a missing session id into a refusal, against the audit's claim that the session-capture cell "has the same shape". The reviewer confirmed the implementer and refuted the audit by reading launcher internals: the session id is extracted from the stream by a fixed jq filter and written BEFORE `exit_code`, so when `exit_code` exists an absent `session_id` means no session event ever appeared. That is not transient - it is a finished measurement with a real negative answer, since the marshal resumes through the same `$RUN_DIR/session_id` file. Converting it to a refusal would have made a route that genuinely cannot resume UNRECORDABLE, trading a true negative for silence, which is worse because nothing then accumulates evidence.

That audit claim had been relayed in the coordinator's brief as established. It was not.

## The one finding worth carrying forward

The implementer flagged that the probe ignores `fire-marshal.sh`'s `THINKING` effort override. The reviewer generalised it: the MODEL axis has the same hole via `MODEL_FORCED` (`fire-marshal.sh:236-261`, `:802`) and was not flagged. So an operator who probes at `gpt-5.6-sol`/`xhigh`, then launches with `--model ...-low` or `--thinking low` to conserve quota during an incident, deploys weaker than the receipt certifies, on exactly the two capability-sensitive cells this milestone made load-bearing.

Bounded today: the override is explicit, printed, and `marshal_receipts.evaluate` has ZERO production callers. Filed as cond-0467 against M5c, which must compare a receipt against the configuration that will actually launch, overrides included. Declining to add the check here was correct rather than lazy: with no caller able to supply an expected model it would have been a check nothing reads, which is the half-built shape `AGENTS.md` forbids.

cond-0388-pr121-review-opus-r1, protocol v2, terminal fbffeb69: the launch response was lost, the handler caught it, the exact-reservation read proved zero admission, and the run recorded state never-started-proven with failure_class response-loss. comments.body:
MERGED. Fork main is now `04adf8764e624d0bc1180e59b866dbcedb20e498` (PR #130). Independent review verdict: **SOUND**, findings minor.

## The result

| run, exact CI invocation | failed | passed | errors |
|---|---|---|---|
| local before | 400 | 10121 | 9 |
| local after | 4 | 10526 | 0 |
| hosted CI, this branch | 4 | 10520 | — |

Hosted run `32046179315` on head `c7d7247`: the four failing ids are exactly the pinned cond-0432 Claude-version assertions, and the pass count is identical to current fork main. Since this change adds no tests, an identical pass count is the expected signature and a DROP would have been the masking tell.

## This issue understated its own blast radius, in two ways

**It was not only reading operator state - it was WRITING THROUGH to it.** `clients/database.py:2277` binds `engine = create_engine(DATABASE_URL...)` at IMPORT time, resolving to `~/.aws/cli-agent-orchestrator` when `CAO_STATE_ROOT` is unset. The reviewer inspected the live scratch root mid-suite and found real test writes - `managed_launch_reservations` 3 rows, `workflow_run_step` 2 rows - and a test that had WRITTEN A `settings.json` into the state root. Pre-change those writes landed in the operator's live database, and a test could rewrite the operator's live `settings.json`. That is undetectable corruption of live state, squarely in the irreversible set. The reviewer confirmed the operator's live DB mtime did not move during its run, so the isolation now holds.

**The `MemoryDisabledError` attribution was wrong for roughly a third of the failures.** About 125 were a path-canonicalization class, unmasked only once memory was enabled: fixtures hardcoding `/Users/colin/.claude/settings.json`, which the restore-contract validator's canonical-realpath check rightly refuses because that path is a dotfile-managed symlink on this machine. Invisible in hosted CI, where the path does not exist at all. The coordinator's filing asserted a single cause it had not established.

## Design: mechanism, and both the implementer and reviewer rejected option (b)

`test/conftest.py` sets `CAO_STATE_ROOT` to a per-session scratch directory before the package is imported, and calls production `init_db()` once so partial runs are self-sufficient. An explicitly exported `CAO_STATE_ROOT` is still honoured as a declared input.

The issue's option (b), skip-when-disabled, was rejected by both passes with the same reasoning: it keys ~400 tests' skip decisions off the same undeclared live input, so a local run would silently verify LESS exactly when the operator disables memory - the machine-dependence and the silently-wrong conclusion both survive - and it does nothing at all about the write-through. The failure this ships is a silently wrong conclusion, and "remember to export an env var" is policy, which is what already failed.

## Two further latent dependencies the isolation surfaced

A **missing-schema** dependency: with a fresh root, `test/services` alone produced 108 failures, because tests using the default engine had been silently relying on the operator's already-migrated live database, or on full-run ordering where an API test boots the app first.

A **process-env scrub leak**: `managed_provider_bridge._serve` scrubs `os.environ` and restores only on return, but three test files run its accept loop in daemon threads that never return, so the scrub stripped `CAO_STATE_ROOT` and everything else for every later test's subprocesses. Fixed with one autouse snapshot/restore fixture at the general seam rather than three site patches, found with a bisecting probe fixture since removed.

## How the review established non-vacuity, which is the part worth imitating

The masking risk in a test-isolation change is that formerly-failing tests now pass without exercising anything. The reviewer did not reason about this - it reproduced the pre-change condition SAFELY, exporting `CAO_STATE_ROOT` at a FAKE operator root containing `{"memory":{"enabled":false}}` with no live-state contact, and got 30 failures with `MemoryDisabledError` raised from INSIDE `memory_service.store/recall`. That is a mutation test on the input rather than the code: the tests fail when the subject is disabled, so their pass under the scratch root is a real exercise.

On skips it produced decisive arithmetic rather than a comparison of pass counts: base `400 + 10121 + 9 = 10530` executed, branch `4 + 10526 + 0 = 10530` executed. Nothing vanished. The diff adds no skip or skipif anywhere, all 15 skips carry pre-existing in-file reasons, and the 13 deselections are the `-m "not e2e"` filter.

It also verified that every migration and unmigrated-store test builds its own engine on `tmp_path` or injects the error synthetically, so the conftest `init_db()` hides nothing; and that the replacement fixture paths still flow through the validator's realpath comparison, with the dot and dotdot refusal cases still refusing.

## Findings carried forward, all minor

`test/e2e/conftest.py:40` removes isolation session-wide when any e2e-marked item is selected, so later non-e2e tests in a combined run lose it. The failure direction is toward visible red rather than hidden green, and the behaviour is documented in the comment.

`test/managed_launch` codex digest patch (`test_managed_launch.py:1052-1067`) monkeypatches `_digest_or_absent` to ignore its `path` argument, so the seam no longer proves the digester is pointed at the right file. The stated property - the probe does not mutate config - is intact. This is the ingredient-versus-wiring pattern in miniature and is worth one line, but it is a test-scope reduction inside a test-infrastructure change rather than a production defect, so it is recorded rather than treated as blocking. That is a deliberate proportionality call: the two residuals blocked earlier tonight sat behind a billing leak and a false attestation respectively.

A residual race remains: the teardown `clear`/`update` can interleave with the never-returning daemon bridge threads' own `os.environ.clear()`. Pre-existing; the fixture strictly reduces the leak window.

comments.body:
OPERATOR DESIGN DIRECTION, and a coordinator correction. This supersedes the two "design consequences" in the filing comment above.

## Correction 1: the budget is ALREADY per-agent. No change needed.

The operator raised that a 3-per-90-minutes cap must be per-agent rather than global, because three agents hitting one API blip would immediately exhaust a shared bucket. That concern is already satisfied by the accepted design: M8-A's budget key is the exact `(CAO session, stable agent_id, task occurrence)`. Three agents hitting the same blip hold three independent budgets. The earlier comment described it as a "shared recovery budget", which was misleading — it is shared between M8 and M9 (so they never keep independent counters), not shared across agents.

## Correction 2: DROP the proxy-versus-provider classifier. It was over-engineering.

Operator direction: there is no reliable way to distinguish a proxy failure from a provider outage other than noticing that both OpenAI and Anthropic traffic degrade simultaneously, and **the correct response is the same either way** — one simple nudge to wake the agent and have it continue. Making the residential proxy connection more stable is a separate problem the operator owns and is not in scope here.

So the classification gate proposed above is dropped. It would have bought an evidence-gate pass and changed no action.

What survives, in weaker form: the record must not **assert provider fault**. Record that transport failed, without attributing cause to the provider. M5b route-eligibility receipts read this evidence, and systematically attributing this installation's network noise to whichever provider happened to be mid-request would poison route decisions. Neutral record, no classifier.

## The substantive design change: count INEFFECTIVE nudges, not nudges

The budget's real job is to bound a mechanism that writes bytes into a live agent. It currently counts nudges, but the thing worth bounding is nudges **that do not work**. A nudge that succeeds costs almost nothing and should consume nothing.

Proposed shape:

- Nudge sent, agent resumes and produces a model turn: **reset the counter to zero.** The occurrence may be nudged again, indefinitely, because every nudge so far is demonstrably productive.
- Nudge sent, no model turn follows: increment. After a small number of CONSECUTIVE ineffective nudges, stop nudging that agent and escalate.

Why this is better than a flat count: on this installation a flaky link produces recurrent blips whose correct response is always the same cheap nudge. A flat cap converts a self-healing situation into a parked worker for the remainder of the window — the automation makes a recoverable condition durable, which is the exact inversion of its purpose and the failure shape `AGENTS.md` now names. Counting ineffectiveness bounds the genuinely dangerous case (a nudge loop burning provider quota against a wedged agent) without penalising the common case.

**The effectiveness signal already exists and needs no new detection.** M10 shipped it: the M10-A/M10-B model-turn receipt convergence, and cond-0422's "prove the retained round became a model turn", are precisely the observation "did this nudge produce a turn". M8 consumes it rather than building anything.

This also dissolves the transient-versus-unresponsive question the operator raised without needing a timer. Duration is a weaker discriminator than effect: transient means the nudge worked, unresponsive means it did not. No 90-minute wall is required to tell them apart.

## Escalation notifies, it does not stop — and it uses a DIFFERENT key

Operator direction: on repeated API errors, alert via `/alert-colin` that the API is unstable and repeatedly crashing, **but keep nudging**. So escalation is notify-only, and it is a separate concern from nudge authority with a separate key:

- **Nudge authority** — keyed per `(session, agent_id, occurrence)`, gated on effectiveness. On threshold: stop nudging THAT agent, escalate.
- **Instability alert** — keyed installation-wide, counting error occurrences across agents. On threshold: alert the operator. Nudging continues unchanged.

Cross-agent aggregation, which was the operator's original worry for the nudge budget, is exactly what is WANTED for the alert: several agents failing at once is the evidence that the cause is infrastructure rather than one bad worker.

## A free diagnostic that answers the operator's own question

The operator states their only means of telling proxy from provider is noticing both OpenAI and Anthropic degrade at the same time. The system can compute that: error occurrences from **two or more distinct providers within a short window** is strong evidence of shared infrastructure rather than a provider incident.

So the instability alert can carry that inference — "this pattern looks like the shared network path, not one provider" — using only aggregation over evidence M6a already emits. No new detector, no new provider work, and it automates the judgement the operator currently makes by eye.

## Still blocked on the same thing

The anchored literal text of each error surface, for Codex/OpenAI and for Claude Code, plus for each whether the harness self-retried and recovered and whether the turn was terminally dead. M6a matches anchored patterns and must not guess. The screenshots did not reach the session; a pasted verbatim line is more useful than an image.

Note that under the ineffective-nudge design the corpus requirement softens usefully: a surface that cannot be confidently classified as self-retrying can be nudged anyway, because a nudge that turns out to be unnecessary is cheap and an unnecessary one that works still resets nothing important. The anchors are still needed to recognise the surface at all.

comments.body:
A REAL CAPTURED INSTANCE of the failure shape this issue is about, observed live on 2026-08-17, with verbatim text. Recording it because it is the same pattern as the proxy case in a different substrate, and it is the first instance in this corpus where the literal strings were captured rather than described.

## What happened

During PR verification, GitHub entered a partial outage (incident `zkxwbgr0cnmx`; the operator's own personal-access-tokens settings page returned `504 - we couldn't respond to your request in time`). The API degraded NON-UNIFORMLY across endpoints, in the same session, with the same credential:

    repos/colindmurray/cao-conductor/actions/runs
      -> {"message":"Resource not accessible by personal access token", "status":"403"}

    gh api user
      -> No server is currently available to service your request. Sorry about that.
         Please try resubmitting your request and contact us if the problem persists. (HTTP 503)

    repos/colindmurray/cli-agent-orchestrator/actions/runs   -> SUCCESS
    repos/colindmurray/cao-conductor                          -> SUCCESS
    repos/colindmurray/cao-conductor/pulls/173                -> SUCCESS
    gh api rate_limit                                         -> SUCCESS, 4998 remaining

## Why this belongs in this issue

**An infrastructure failure presented as a PERMISSION error.** The 403 text names the personal access token as the cause. It is not the cause. The same endpoint had succeeded repeatedly minutes earlier on the same token, and the identical call against a different repository continued to succeed throughout.

That is structurally identical to the residential-proxy case this issue was opened for: a shared-infrastructure failure wearing the clothes of a component-specific fault. In the proxy case it wears a provider's error surface; here it wore an authorization error.

**The 403 was CONSISTENT while the 503 was intermittent, and the consistency was misleading.** A detector — or a coordinator — that weights "reproducible on retry" as evidence of a real permission state will reach the wrong conclusion. Reproducibility distinguishes nothing during a partial outage, because a degraded route degrades every time it is taken.

**The coordinator got this wrong in exactly the way the design is meant to prevent.** Having a 503 in hand, which is unambiguously server-side, it discounted it because the 403 reproduced, and asserted a per-repository fine-grained-PAT permission gap as the mechanism. The remediation that wrong mechanism implied was to EDIT TOKEN SCOPES during an outage. That is the concrete harm of inferring cause from status codes: the action it recommends is not merely useless but damaging, and it is aimed at the operator's credentials.

## What this confirms about the design already recorded here

1. **Do not infer cause from status codes or from error text that names a cause.** M6a's insistence on anchored literal patterns plus a closed `recovery_action` enum is correct, and this instance shows why: the error string itself asserted a false cause with high confidence.
2. **Cross-signal correlation is the discriminator, and it worked.** The only reliable tell was several endpoints disagreeing at the same moment on the same credential. That is precisely the multi-provider correlation proposed above for the instability alert, in a different substrate, and it is the signal that resolved this once it was actually consulted.
3. **Neutral recording, not attribution.** Had this been recorded as a provider fault or a permission fault, both would have been wrong. Recording "the call did not reach a serving endpoint" would have been right in both readings.
4. **Passive wait was the correct handling, and the nudge-equivalent was correctly withheld.** No merge was performed against an unverifiable gate, and no credential was touched. The recovery is to retry once the incident clears, with no state change in between.

## Corpus value

Anchored literal candidates from this instance, both verbatim above: the `Resource not accessible by personal access token` 403 body, and the `No server is currently available to service your request` 503 text. Note the second is a plausible generic-transport anchor, while the FIRST MUST NOT be treated as a permission fact — if anything it argues that an authorization-shaped error needs corroboration from a second endpoint before it is classified at all.

The two provider error surfaces originally requested for this issue, Codex/OpenAI and Claude Code, are still outstanding; the screenshots did not reach the session and pasted verbatim text is what the evidence gate needs.

## Codex / OpenAI — two lines, and they are a PAIR

Captured twice, two minutes apart (09:57:40 and 09:58:37 local), byte-identical both times, so this recurs rather than being a one-off:

    ⚠ Falling back from WebSockets to HTTPS transport. request timed out
    ■ request timed out

THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THIS CAPTURE: the two lines are different states, and the screen distinguishes them without inference.

The `⚠` line IS Codex's self-retry, visible as it happens — it is switching transport from WebSockets to HTTPS in response to the timeout. That is the `self-retrying` class, and the correct action is to do nothing.

The bare `■ request timed out` is the state AFTER the fallback also failed. That is the terminal class.

So a detector can read "still trying" versus "gave up" off the screen. The M6a taxonomy needed exactly this discrimination and it was assumed to require inference or timing; Codex surfaces it directly. Note the ordering matters: a `request timed out` following a fallback warning is terminal, whereas the fallback warning alone means recovery is in progress.

## Claude Code — a NEW anchor, distinct from the one already tracked

    ● API Error: Connection refused – a firewall or proxy may be blocking it (ConnectionRefused)
    ● 2 background commands completed
    ● API Error: Connection refused – a firewall or proxy may be blocking it (ConnectionRefused)

Note the en dash `–`, not a hyphen, and the parenthesised `(ConnectionRefused)` error class. Note also that it appears TWICE in one screen with work completing between, which is the repetition the operator described.

THIS IS NOT THE LINE ALREADY IN cond-0307. That issue carries:

    API Error: Connection closed mid-response. The response above may be incomplete.

The two are different states with different safety properties:

- `Connection closed mid-response` — the connection died DURING a response, so partial output exists and the turn's effects are ambiguous. cond-0307's own text warns that the response above may be incomplete.
- `Connection refused (ConnectionRefused)` — the connection NEVER ESTABLISHED. The turn definitively did not proceed, no bytes were produced, and no effect can be half-applied. That makes it the SAFEST possible nudge candidate in the whole corpus: there is nothing to double-execute.

M6a's executing allowlist should treat them as separate patterns with the same `recovery_action=nudge` but different confidence, since the refused case carries no partial-effect risk at all.

## The provider's own text declines to blame the provider

`a firewall or proxy may be blocking it` — Claude Code itself points outward, at the network path, not at Anthropic.

That materially simplifies the attribution concern raised earlier in this issue. The proposed proxy-versus-provider classifier was already dropped as over-engineering on operator direction, since the action is identical either way. This capture shows the concern was smaller still: the error string does not assert provider fault, so recording it verbatim neither defames a provider nor requires a classifier. Record the line; it is already honest about not knowing.

## The cross-provider correlation is now empirically demonstrated

Codex failed at 09:57:40 and again at 09:58:37. Claude Code failed at 09:59:43. Two different providers, two different error surfaces, inside roughly two minutes.

That is precisely the discriminator proposed above for the instability alert — error occurrences from two or more distinct providers within a short window as evidence of shared infrastructure rather than a provider incident — and it is confirmed by the operator's own capture rather than by argument. The operator stated that noticing both providers degrade simultaneously is their only means of telling proxy from provider; this capture is an instance of exactly that judgement, and it is computable from the evidence M6a already emits.

## Corpus entries, ready for the M6a evidence gate

| provider | anchored pattern | turn_state | recovery_action | note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| codex | `Falling back from WebSockets to HTTPS transport` | self-retrying | ignore | recovery in progress; a transport switch, not a failure |
| codex | `request timed out` following the fallback warning | terminal | nudge | the fallback also failed |
| claude | `API Error: Connection refused` / `(ConnectionRefused)` | terminal | nudge | connection never established; no partial effect possible |
| claude | `API Error: Connection closed mid-response` | terminal | nudge | already in cond-0307 and in M6a's allowlist; partial output possible |

What still needs confirming before the Codex rows execute, and only the operator can answer it from what they observed: whether the Codex turn was terminally dead after the bare `request timed out`, or whether it eventually resumed on its own. The screen ordering strongly suggests terminal, since the fallback was the retry and it failed, but that is an inference from layout rather than an observation of the outcome.

## One capture in the set is not an agent error

The fourth screenshot is GitHub's 504 interstitial — "We couldn't respond to your request in time." — which is the operator's evidence for incident `zkxwbgr0cnmx`, not a provider surface. Recorded here only so the set is accounted for.
