issues.body:
Severity: P2. Repository: cli-agent-orchestrator. Every pull request against fork `main` is currently red because of this, so it blocks the green-CI merge threshold repository-wide.

DEFECT. Four tests assert an EXACT Claude version set of `['2.1.220']`, but the route now accepts `2.1.233` alongside it. The assertion visible in the hosted job log is:

    assert ['2.1.233', '2.1.220'] == ['2.1.220']

FAILING TESTS, identical on `main` and on every branch built from it:

    test/api/test_managed_launch_api.py::test_capability_handshake_is_exact_and_versioned
    test/services/test_claude_native_adapter.py::TestCapabilityAdvertisement::test_the_advertised_versions_are_an_exact_set
    test/services/test_managed_launch.py::TestRouteAttestationDispatchesByProvider::test_a_drifted_claude_build_is_refused
    test/services/test_recovery_contracts.py::test_pinned_versions

ORIGIN. Two commits on `main` widened the accepted Claude build set without updating these four exact-set assertions: `74194107` "fix(provider): accept Claude 2.1.233 alongside 2.1.220 (retain 2.1.220 for minted sessions)" and `62df9369` "fix(route): allow any semver Claude version when open enforcement (unpin)". Both belong to the separately owned goal-lifecycle campaign rather than to Fire Marshal, which is why this is filed rather than fixed here.

EVIDENCE, from hosted CI job logs rather than local runs. Base `main` `62df9369`, run `31962985593`: 4 failed, 10406 passed. An unrelated feature branch head, run `31976008182`: 4 failed, 10412 passed. Sorted failing-id sets are byte-identical, with `comm` empty in both directions. The pass delta of exactly six accounts for that branch's six added tests and nothing else moved. Fork `main` history shows the same red state persisting: `62df9369` fail, `e52a0cad` fail, `51c1aadb` success, `681c1bb1` fail, `fadfbabb` fail.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE FOUR TESTS. The accepted merge threshold is exact-head CI green with no reproduced P0/P1. With `main` red, every PR must instead prove that its failures are precisely main's pre-existing set, which is materially harder, requires job-log retrieval, and invites the good-enough rule to be stretched. It also masks genuine regressions: a fifth failure appearing in the same run is easy to miss against four expected ones.

A NOTE ON DIAGNOSIS, recorded because it cost real time. `gh pr checks` and the `check-runs` REST endpoint both return 403 "Resource not accessible by personal access token" for the fine-grained PAT in use, but the `actions/runs` and `actions/runs/{id}/jobs` endpoints work, and job logs are retrievable with `gh api --allow-escape-sequences repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/jobs/<job_id>/logs`. Without that flag the log request appears to fail in a way easily mistaken for a permissions problem.

FIX DIRECTION, not prescribed. The four assertions should express the intended contract rather than a frozen literal. If the route genuinely accepts any semver under open enforcement, an exact-set assertion is the wrong shape and should assert the enforcement rule; if a pinned set is still intended for minted sessions specifically, the assertions should say which set applies to which path. Whoever owns the unpin should decide, because the right answer depends on what the unpin was for.

ACCEPTANCE. Fork `main` returns to green, and the four tests fail if the accepted-version contract regresses rather than merely if a literal changes.
issues.title: four exact-set Claude version assertions left behind by the route unpin keep fork main red

issues.body:
Severity: P1. Repository: cli-agent-orchestrator. Present in MERGED code at `e644c65a5b9001b8178b0864f6ccaa07cf62c892` (M3-E E1, PR #126). Not currently biting the operator's live installation; see blast radius below.

DEFECT. `_migrate_task_occurrence_handoffs()` (`clients/database.py:3273`) creates the table with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` (`:3287`) and has NO column-evolution path. It does not call the house helper `_add_columns_if_missing`, which exists in the same module and is the established pattern for exactly this. A store whose `task_occurrence_handoffs` table was created by an earlier M3-E build keeps the old shape indefinitely, because `IF NOT EXISTS` is a no-op against an existing table of any shape.

WHY THAT IS A P1 RATHER THAN A MIGRATION NICETY. The hold is enforced at `control_input_service.py:445` via `task_handoff.hold_refusal_for_terminal(...)`, near the top of `provider_byte_admission`, which gates all three managed write lanes. `hold_refusal` fails closed on any `TaskHandoffError`. So a shape-drifted table makes every query against it raise, and the fail-closed path then REFUSES EVERY MANAGED WRITE ON THE INSTALLATION -- every steer, tell, and operator message -- for agents that are party to no handoff at all, and types the refusal `handoff-held`, asserting that a handback is pending. That reason code was introduced precisely to prevent that confusion, so the failure mode actively misdirects diagnosis.

The two halves of M3-E have different exposure and the record should say so: the route/API half is genuinely dark, because nothing calls the handoff routes and the conductor has no client method. The ENFORCEMENT half is LIVE on every managed write from the moment of merge. The kill switch is therefore the hold call, not the router registration.

BLAST RADIUS TODAY. The operator's live control-input store does not contain `task_occurrence_handoffs` at all, so the next `init_db()` creates it fresh at the correct shape and the live installation is not exposed. The reachable cases are: any state root created by a development run against the pre-repair E1 tree, whose schema is mutually incompatible with the merged one; and any FUTURE shape change to this table, which will strand every store created before it. `init_db()` runs on every fork server start, so the drift is silent until the first managed write is refused.

PRECEDENT ALREADY IN THE MODULE. `_migrate_stable_agent_roster` carries defensive rebuild logic explicitly for "a database that ran the earlier dark draft". M3-E omits the equivalent.

FIX DIRECTION. Use the house column-evolution helper so an existing table gains missing columns rather than being silently accepted at the wrong shape, or detect a shape mismatch and rebuild as the roster migration does. Whichever is chosen, a shape mismatch must not present as `handoff-held`: a store that cannot answer the hold question is not a store reporting a pending handback, and the refusal reason should say so.

ACCEPTANCE. A store created at an earlier M3-E shape is migrated or rebuilt on `init_db()`; managed writes succeed for agents party to no handoff; and any residual unreadable-store condition produces a typed reason distinct from `handoff-held`.

PROVENANCE. Found by an integration reviewer grading the branch tip after its own session had been superseded; both structural claims independently verified by the coordinator against the merged tree -- the migration's lack of `_add_columns_if_missing`, and the `hold_refusal_for_terminal` call site at `control_input_service.py:445`. The post-merge audit for this merge is deferred on Z.ai quota, so no other scheduled pass covers this tree.

Related: cond-0381 (M3-E, remains open pending E2).
issues.resolution: fixed
issues.title: M3-E handoff-table migration has no column-evolution path; a drifted shape refuses every managed write as handoff-held

issues.body:
## Symptom

`tests/test_marshal_session.LauncherCommitBoundaryTest.test_a_child_that_ignores_sigterm_does_not_survive_the_cleanup`
fails non-deterministically. It spawns a real child that ignores SIGTERM and
waits for the cleanup to reap it; under machine load the wait expires before
the child exits.

## Classification (baseline before attribution)

Run in isolation, three times each, on the same machine:

- clean `origin/main` @ affd998: OK, OK, FAILED
- an unrelated feature branch on top of it: FAILED, FAILED, OK

Non-deterministic on BOTH, so it is base-existing and flaky rather than caused
by any branch under test. It surfaced during a full-suite run on a busy host,
which is exactly the condition that makes a real-process timing assertion
marginal.

Distinct from the recorded local-only failure
`test_gc_workspaces.GcWorkspacesTest.test_collected_clean_run_reapable`,
which fails deterministically 3/3 locally and passes in CI. This one fails
intermittently everywhere it was tried.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than recording

A flaky test in the cleanup path is worse than an ordinary flake: cleanup is
the thing operators trust to have actually happened, and a test that passes
most of the time trains readers to retry rather than investigate. The next
genuine cleanup regression would look identical to this noise.

## Suggested direction

Make the wait bounded by an observable rather than a duration - poll for the
child's exit with a generous ceiling and fail only when the process is still
alive at the end - or mark the timing assertion explicitly load-sensitive so a
failure names the condition rather than the behaviour.
issues.title: marshal session cleanup test is load-flaky (base-existing, non-deterministic on main)

issues.body:
## Symptom

`conduct successor dispose` cannot succeed against any target in any project.
Every census reports `ledger` and `shim` as `unknown`, so `observation_complete`
is always false, `releasable` is always false, and the verb returns exit 65
(`claim-observation-incomplete`) unconditionally.

The remedies the census names for those unknowns are not executable, so the
operator has no forward move. COND-0431 replaced a permanent dead end with a
retryable one; it is still a dead end.

## Mechanism

### 1. `ledger` / `shim` truthiness bug — the verb is inert everywhere

`successor_policy_registry.artifact_projection()` normalizes every artifact
kind into a wrapper dict, present whether or not the kind is bound:

    {"required": False, "expected_identity": None, "expected_identity_sha256": None}

`_successor.py` probes bindingness by the truthiness of that wrapper:

    bound = artifacts.get(key)
    probes[name] = _q_row("not-applicable", ..., evidence={"bound": bool(bound)}) \
        if not bound else _q_row("unknown", ..., note=f"this attempt binds a {name} ...")

The wrapper is a non-empty dict in every case, so `bool(bound)` is always
`True`. `ledger` and `shim` therefore report `unknown` for every attempt ever
recorded. The adjacent comment states the intended rule correctly — "Kinds this
attempt does not bind are not-applicable ... a surface with no binding has
nothing to be live through" — and the code does not implement it.

`launch-breaker` reads `not-applicable` only incidentally: it looks up
`launch_breaker`, which is not in `ARTIFACT_KINDS`, so `.get()` returns `None`.
Right answer, wrong reason.

Correct predicate is `required is True` (equivalently, a non-null
`expected_identity`), not the presence of the projection wrapper.

`tests/test_successor_dispose_probes.py:176` builds `{"artifacts": {"ledger":
{"bound": True}}}` — a shape `artifact_projection()` never produces. The fixture
invented its own schema, so the bug was invisible to the suite.

### 2. `shim` has a real probe that is never called

`conduct.lib.shims.route_entry(project_state_dir, worktree_realpath)` is a
direct read of the authoritative route map, and `cleanup_route()` is its
teardown. The census consults neither, and reports `unknown` with the note
"this attempt binds a shim this version does not probe" — which is false; this
version does probe it, elsewhere.

Observed on `cond-0388-report-chain-reconciliation-fix-deepseek-r3`: the
project's `routes.json` is present and readable with 62 entries and holds no
entry for that attempt's worktree. That is a considered negative answer from the
store's own liveness test — exactly what the design requires — and the census
discards it.

### 3. `provider-process` names an impossible remedy

The r3 journal never bound a terminal id, so `_probe_terminal` returns
`not-applicable`. `_TERMINAL_IMPLIES_NO_PROCESS` covers only `absent` and
`disposed`, so `_apply_provider_process_rule` downgrades provider-process to
`unknown` and names:

    end the terminal through ordinary lifecycle work
    (conduct retire / conduct collect / conduct spawn --recover)
    until it answers absent, then dispose again

There is no terminal to end. The supervisor followed this instruction and
`conduct retire` refused because the run is already finalized as `failed`. The
refusal is correct; the remedy was never applicable.

Refusing to derive absence here is defensible — `terminal_id` is journaled from
the CAO create response, so a crash between pane creation and journaling leaves
an unjournaled pane. But then the remedy must be an operation that can actually
settle it: enumerate the peer's terminals and look for one bound to this
attempt's identity (worktree, reservation id, task id). An exhaustive negative
from a live peer is a considered answer; an unreachable peer is `unknown` with
"restore the CAO peer", which is executable.

### 4. `remedy_precondition_holds` is a hardcoded constant

The field is documented as evidence that "a `live` row must name a command whose
precondition the probe confirmed on the record it just read." It is assigned at
13 sites and every one is the literal `True`. Nothing computes it.

`_downgrade_unremediable()` — rule (b), the mechanism that turns an unactionable
`live` into an escapable `unknown` — gates on
`row.get("remedy_precondition_holds") is True` and therefore can never fire. It
is dead code.

This is also why `tests/test_successor_no_dead_ends.py` passed while shipping a
dead end: it asserts a remedy *string* is present and that no verdict is both
un-overridable and un-remediable. It never asserts the named remedy is
applicable to the target's actual lifecycle state, and a hardcoded `True`
satisfies every check it makes.

## Observed

    conduct successor show --project p1-closure \
      --task-id cond-0388-report-chain-reconciliation-fix-deepseek-r3

    unknown: ["ledger", "provider-process", "shim"]
    releasable: false   disposable: false   observation_complete: false

Ground truth for the same target:

    ledger  -> registry says required=false, expected_identity=null  (nothing bound)
    shim    -> routes.json readable, 62 entries, no entry for this worktree
    lease   -> disposed        seat -> released       terminal -> never bound

All three unknowns are answerable from records already on disk.

## Why it matters

1. The verb shipped inert. `dispose` has never been able to return
   `would_dispose=true` for any target, so COND-0431's stated remedy does not
   exist in practice and COND-0388 r3's source is still fenced.
2. It reproduces the exact defect COND-0431 was filed to fix. "Not defined in
   this version" became "this version does not probe", and a missing observation
   is again reported as a property of the claim.
3. The anti-dead-end regression test is satisfied by a constant, so the
   guarantee it advertises is not in force for any surface.

## Suggested direction

- Probe bindingness by `required`/`expected_identity`, not by the presence of
  the projection wrapper; assert against a real `artifact_projection()` result
  in the test rather than a hand-built fixture.
- Wire `shims.route_entry()` as the shim probe: no entry is `absent`, an entry
  matching this attempt is `live` with `cleanup_route` as the remedy, an entry
  matching a different attempt is `custody-elsewhere`.
- Give `provider-process` an enumeration probe for the never-bound-terminal
  case, and make its remedy one the operator can run.
- Compute `remedy_precondition_holds` from the record just read at every site,
  and add a check that fails if any call site passes a literal.
- Extend the no-dead-ends matrix to assert applicability, not just presence:
  a named remedy must resolve to a verb that is legal against the target's
  current lifecycle state.
issues.resolution: [ALREADY-FIXED] Commit 463753d 'fix(successor): make claim disposition able to succeed at all' plus follow-up d97b394 'read the pane binding where it is written, and both launch surfaces' (`git log -S'remedy_precondition_holds' -- conduct/`). Current main: conduct/commands/_successor.py:3475 and :3616 read `registry_lib.artifact_binding(attempt, key)` instead of the projection wrapper's truthiness (`grep -n 'bool(bound)' conduct/commands/_successor.py` returns nothing); :1540/:1595/:3036 call `_shims().shim_identity_digest(...)` and :3504 `shims.route_entry(psd, worktree)`; :3366-3367 `remedy_precondition="the target run is not already finalized", remedy_precondition_holds=(finalized is False)` and :3535-3539 `(entry is not None or token_present)` — no longer all literal True. tests/test_successor_dispose_probes.py:342 builds `registry_lib.artifact_projection(**projection)` (the real constructor), :353 test_an_unbound_kind_is_not_applicable_under_the_real_projection, :363 test_a_quiet_attempt_can_actually_reach_releasable, :137 test_an_inapplicable_remedy_downgrades_live_to_unknown. | All five items in the issue's own suggested direction landed: bindingness from artifact_binding rather than the wrapper, shim wired to the route map's own liveness test, provider-process resolved through the managed-launch reservation (where a stalled launch actually records its terminal) instead of only the journal, remedy_precondition_holds computed at the sites where it can be false, and the no-dead-ends matrix extended with the two invariants that make an inert verb visible — releasable must be reachable from production probes, and the downgrade rule must actually fire. The issue's own c | Vetted 2026-08-17 against origin/main 1f0b8a6 in an 8-agent sweep of all 64 open P0/P1 issues; every remove/soften recommendation was independently spot-checked against source.
issues.title: successor dispose is inert: ledger/shim always unknown, and the remedy-applicability guard is a constant

issues.body:
## Symptom

Managed recovery refuses for every journaled run whose pinned Python
interpreter file no longer exists on disk. `_verified_recovery_command` opens
`argv[0]` to re-hash it, the open fails, and the sentinel raises rather than
recovering — the same silent-until-deadman failure as COND-0424, from a
different cause.

## Mechanism

`sourcechain.runtime_recovery_command` pins `argv[0]` to
`realpath(sys.executable)`, which under uv is a versioned path:

    /Users/colin/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.13.15-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.13

Upgrading or garbage-collecting a uv-managed Python removes that exact
directory. The pin then names a file that is not there, and every run journaled
against it is permanently unrecoverable. Nothing rebinds it, and nothing
reports it.

`plugin/conductor_sentinel/sentinel.py::_verified_recovery_command`:

    real = os.path.realpath(argv[0])
    with open(real, "rb") as fh:                  # <- OSError, not a refusal
        observed = hashlib.sha256(fh.read()).hexdigest()

The `OSError` propagates as-is, so this case is not even reported as an
identity refusal; it surfaces as an unhandled read error from the recovery
path.

## Observed

Across the whole conductor state root on this host, every journal carrying a
runtime `recovery_command` was classified by re-running the sentinel's own
predicate:

    journaled runs with a runtime recovery_command : 229
      interpreter file is gone                     : 207
      tree drift (COND-0424, fixed separately)     :  22

Of the 207, **102 are not finalized**, and roughly 30 are in states that still
expect to be driven — 27 `submitted`, 2 `preflight-blocked`, 1 `created`.

The interpreter these journals name is absent while a different uv-managed
CPython is present, so this is an interpreter upgrade, not a host migration.

## Relationship to COND-0424

They are siblings, not duplicates. COND-0424 is the *package tree* pin breaking
on every `conduct install`; its fix re-anchors that pin to the live deploy
receipt and restores all 22 affected runs. This is the *interpreter* pin
breaking when the interpreter itself is replaced, and the COND-0424 fix
deliberately does not touch it: the interpreter identity is the safety property
that keeps the sentinel from executing something that is not the conductor.

## Why it matters

The two together mean managed recovery currently verifies for **0 of 229**
journaled runs on this host. The COND-0424 fix raises that to 22. This issue is
the rest.

## Suggested direction

- Distinguish the cases: a missing interpreter should be a typed refusal naming
  the absent path, never a bare `OSError` out of the recovery path.
- Consider rebinding to the interpreter the live deploy receipt vouches for,
  the way COND-0424 re-anchors the tree pin. The deploy receipt records
  `executables.conduct` but not the interpreter behind it, so this likely needs
  the receipt to record the interpreter identity as well.
- Report at deploy time how many journaled, non-finalized runs the newly
  installed toolchain has just made unrecoverable, so the loss is visible at
  the moment it happens rather than at a deadman weeks later.
- Whatever the shape, an interpreter upgrade should not silently remove the
  recovery net from every running lane.
issues.title: a replaced Python interpreter permanently disarms managed recovery for every run journaled against it

issues.body:
## Symptom

The sentinel still presents cancelled human gates as pending. COND-0421 gave a
cancelled authorization its own state, but the fix landed only in
`conduct/lib/workstate.py`. The sentinel runs a vendored copy,
`plugin/conductor_sentinel/_workstate.py`, which was never re-synced — so the
one surface that autonomously alerts and nudges about outstanding human gates
kept inviting the forbidden action.

## Mechanism

`plugin/conductor_sentinel/_workstate.py` is a verbatim vendored copy of the
canonical module below its inlined block, modulo eight declared name rewrites.
Commit `6eb9c83` ("fix(gate): give a cancelled authorization its own state")
changed the canonical and not the copy:

    conduct/lib/workstate.py                  6eb9c83, 78c77b7, e5d08df
    plugin/conductor_sentinel/_workstate.py            78c77b7, e5d08df

The vendored `_scan_gates` therefore never reads `gate.cancelled.json` and has
no `cancelled` branch, so a cancelled gate falls through to
`"pending" if approval is missing`.

`plugin/tests/test_workstate_vendor.py::SourceDriftTest` exists precisely to
catch this and **is currently failing on `origin/main`** at `e7f44b5`. Its
docstring says why: *"a claim in a docstring that nothing checks is how a
vendored module drifts."* The check worked; the failure shipped anyway.

## Observed

Running both copies against live `p1-closure` state, same inputs:

    gate cond-0225-0230-pr83-reviewer-opus-to-sol-high-412255c0-d7e7-446f-b1ee-027a60188cb8

    deployed vendored copy : state='pending'    since=2026-08-10T03:48:53Z
    re-vendored copy       : state='cancelled'  since=2026-08-16T22:04:09Z
                             sources now include gate.cancelled.json

That gate is the one COND-0421 was filed about. Campaign policy records it
cancelled with outcome `successor-cancelled` and states it must not be
approved, consumed, or replayed. `conduct status` reports it correctly. The
sentinel does not.

No other gate's derived state changes, so the drift is exactly the cancellation
branch and nothing else.

## Why it matters

1. The sentinel is the autonomous surface. `conduct status` is read when a
   human looks; the sentinel alerts, nudges, and drives recovery on its own. Of
   the two, it is the worse one to leave wrong.
2. It presents a forbidden action as a decision the operator still owes, which
   is the exact failure COND-0421 was filed to remove.
3. A phantom-pending human gate is indistinguishable from a real one, so it can
   block or misdirect campaign progress indefinitely.

## Fix

Re-copy the canonical body from the `SNAPSHOT_SCHEMA` anchor and re-apply the
eight declared substitutions, which is what the drift test's failure message
instructs. No behavioural code is written by hand; the vendoring contract
defines the result exactly.

## Follow-up worth considering

The drift test is only as good as someone running the plugin suite. The main
suite (`tests/`) and the plugin suite (`plugin/tests/`) are separate discovery
roots, and a change to `conduct/lib/` does not obviously call for running the
second. Either the canonical-side suite should assert the vendored copy is in
sync, or `conduct deploy` should refuse a build whose vendored modules have
drifted — the same shape as the disposed-claim downgrade guard.
issues.resolution: [ALREADY-FIXED] `git log --oneline -3 -- plugin/conductor_sentinel/_workstate.py` -> a448bee 'fix(sentinel): re-sync the vendored work-state copy so cancelled gates read as cancelled' (merged as 74a9988, PR #165). The vendored copy now reads gate.cancelled.json and has both cancelled branches: plugin/conductor_sentinel/_workstate.py:1957-1958, :1992-1993, :2086-2087, mirroring conduct/lib/workstate.py:1697-1698, :1732-1733, :1826-1827. The drift test the issue reports failing now passes: `PYTHONPATH=plugin:. python -m unittest tests.test_workstate_vendor` -> Ran 31 tests, OK (SourceDriftTest and VocabularyParityTest included). | The exact defect — the vendored `_scan_gates` having no cancelled branch so a cancelled gate fell through to 'pending' — is repaired by re-vendoring, and the drift test that exists to catch it is green on current main. The issue's 'follow-up worth considering' (have the canonical suite or `conduct deploy` assert vendor sync, so the drift test is not only as good as someone remembering to run the plugin suite) is a separate, still-unfiled item; file it on its own if wanted rather than keeping this issue open for it. | Vetted 2026-08-17 against origin/main 1f0b8a6 in an 8-agent sweep of all 64 open P0/P1 issues; every remove/soften recommendation was independently spot-checked against source.
issues.title: the sentinel still reads cancelled gates as pending: vendored _workstate never re-synced after cond-0421

Task/goal lifecycle implementation-plan **PR 9A** — the conductor-owned communication and
attachment catalog in the per-project semantic store.

PR 9 is delivered as four separately reviewable PRs. This issue owns **9A only**:

- schema v5 tables for content blobs, documents, communications, attachments and delivery;
- the capture/snapshot library (assignment-input, file-snapshot, inline-message, promoted-message)
  with exact-stored-byte hashing after any redaction, size budgets, and content dedup;
- reader CLI (`conduct communication show`, `conduct attachment read`);
- the `conduct report` producer seam, so the catalog has a real producer; and
- backfill of existing run reports as file-snapshot communications, never synthesising bytes.

Out of scope: the orchestrator HTTP catalog API (9B), the dashboard Markdown viewer (9C), the
project-wide communications view (9D), and the operator purge command.

Prerequisites are satisfied: the plan gates 9A on PR 1's identity/database seam and PR 2's
task/goal associations, both merged. Verified against plan text and git in both repositories.

Base: `74a99884` (`origin/main`).
issues.resolution: Triage 2026-08-21 vs vision + main 13bcdcc: Verified already-fixed on conductor main. Fix commit/proof cited in triage comment (see prior comment_id). Live file inspection (git log -S, grep) confirms defect absent. Vision: check now correctly scoped/closed; smallest check shipped. No further action. If re-observed, reopen with current file:line.

issues.body:
Severity: P2. Repository: cli-agent-orchestrator. Present in MERGED code at `e644c65a` (M3-E E1, PR #126). Dark today, LIVE the moment E2 wires a conductor caller.

DEFECT. `donor_revision` is recorded at `begin` time, not at the moment the packet digest was taken.

`services/task_handoff.py:697` sets `donor_revision=int(donor["revision"])` inside `_begin_once`. The column comment says it is "the revision the packet digest describes. A transfer compares it." It is not. The caller computes `packet_digest` BEFORE calling begin; begin then reads whatever revision the occurrence happens to carry at begin time. `BeginRequest` has no expected-revision field and the API actively rejects one - `test_unknown_body_fields_are_rejected_rather_than_ignored` pins that a begin body carrying `expected_revision` returns 422. So a caller has no way to pin the revision its digest actually describes.

COOPERATIVE FAILURE SEQUENCE (stale observation across the observe-then-begin window):

1. The donor's turn ends; `record_boundary` bumps its occurrence to revision N.
2. The supervisor observes quiescence, builds the catch-up packet describing revision N, and digests it.
3. Before `begin_handoff` lands, a still-admitted write - the hold does not exist yet - lets the donor's next turn record another boundary, moving it to N+1. The suite itself blesses boundary writes during this window as ordinary (`test_a_held_donor_still_record_a_boundary`).
4. `begin_handoff` records `donor_revision = N+1` against a packet that describes N. Delivery and transfer proceed; the transfer-time revision check compares the donor against N+1 and PASSES.

REPRODUCED against the merged service layer on a scratch SQLite store:

Severity: P2. Repository: cli-agent-orchestrator. Present in MERGED code at `e644c65a` (M3-E E1, PR #126). Dark today, LIVE the moment E2 wires a conductor caller.

DEFECT. "The recipient must be free" is checked once at begin and never enforced for the rest of the handoff window.

`services/task_handoff.py:656-662` performs the begin-time `open_occurrence_for_agent` check. `services/task_occurrence.py:595-639` (`_open_once`) carries no handoff predicate, and the live route `POST /sessions/{session_name}/task-occurrences` (`api/task_occurrence.py:224`) can open a round for that agent at any point afterwards.

The begin-time comment justifies checking there because it is "the last point at which refusing is free - past this the recipient is held and the catch-up packet is typed into its context." But the hold gates BYTES only. Opening an occurrence is a store operation and nothing in `open_occurrence` consults the handoff table.

COOPERATIVE FAILURE SEQUENCE (check-then-act across a long window):

1. The supervisor begins a handback to dormant agent B. B is free, so begin succeeds.
2. An independent dispatch - the conductor's ordinary task assignment, or a response-loss retry of one - opens a new round for B through the occurrence API. This is legal today and takes no lock the handoff holds.
3. The packet is delivered to B. Typed bytes are irreversible by design.
4. `complete_handoff` calls `open_occurrence` for B and raises `TaskOccurrenceConflict: stable agent ... already has open task occurrence ...`. That error type is deliberately not retried by `_with_session`, and retrying could never succeed while B's unrelated round stays open.

REPRODUCED against the merged service layer on a scratch SQLite store:

    transfer refused: TaskOccurrenceConflict: stable agent 68523572-... already has open task occurrence bccb5fa3-...
    handoff still: pending, recipient hold: True, recipient_briefed=True packet already typed

STATE-INTEGRITY IMPACT. A double wedge. The handoff is stuck pending with BOTH agents held, and B's unrelated new round is simultaneously unsteerable because B is handoff-held - after B has already been told in its own context that it is taking over the handback task. Recovery exists: rollback surfaces `recipient_briefed=True` so the cancellation is owed. But the design's stated reason for checking at begin - that refusing there is free - is falsified by the window.

SMALLEST COHERENT REPAIR. Have `open_occurrence`, or the dispatch path that calls it, refuse when the agent is the recipient of a pending handoff, so the invariant the begin-time check establishes stays true until settle.

WHY NO TEST CATCHES IT. No test opens an occurrence for the recipient mid-window.

issues.body:
Severity: P2. Repository: cli-agent-orchestrator. Present in MERGED code at `e644c65a` (M3-E E1, PR #126). Dark today, LIVE the moment E2 wires a conductor caller.

DEFECT. The delivered-to incarnation is caller-asserted and never checked against the roster or against `to_agent_id`.

`services/task_handoff.py:748-818` (`_record_delivery_once`) and `:927-944` (`_complete_once`); API surface at `api/task_handoff.py:186-192` and `:227-232`.

The only validation on the delivery incarnation is that it differs from the donor's `from_incarnation_id`. The only validation at transfer is that it equals the recorded delivery incarnation. The chain therefore verifies that the caller is CONSISTENT, never that it is RIGHT. The module's own docstring states that "the supervisor's roster view can be stale", and the roster (`stable_agent_roster.get_incarnation_by_terminal`, and the incarnation-to-agent binding) is the one authority that could check the assertion. It is consulted on neither write.

COOPERATIVE FAILURE SEQUENCE (stale observation recorded as durable fact):

1. The supervisor delivers the packet, then records delivery naming incarnation `inc-X`, its stale belief about which pane belongs to the recipient. `inc-X` is actually agent C's pane, or a dead one.
2. Transfer names the same `inc-X`. Every check passes: `inc-X` differs from the donor's incarnation, `inc-X` equals the recorded incarnation, and the revisions agree.
3. The successor occurrence for agent B is durably stamped with `incarnation_id=inc-X` and `terminal_id=term-X` - another worker's pane.

REPRODUCED against the merged service layer on a scratch SQLite store:

    transfer outcome: transferred; successor occurrence agent=8726930c... stamped with
    incarnation_id=inc-9 terminal_id=term-9 (never verified to belong to the recipient)

STATE-INTEGRITY IMPACT. The open occurrence is the record every later reader trusts for "who executes this task, on which pane". This binds B's task authority to a pane that is not B's. The module docstring itself names why that is dangerous: `retire_worker_pane` and `admit_fresh_successor` "read by agent and then finalize by occurrence id with no `agent_id` predicate", so recovery acting on this occurrence can finalize or tear down against the wrong physical worker.

SMALLEST COHERENT REPAIR. At `record_packet_delivery`, or at transfer, resolve the incarnation through the roster and refuse unless it belongs to `row.to_agent_id`. The roster read already exists on this seam's hot path and already fails closed there, so this adds no new dependency.

WHY NO TEST CATCHES IT. In every existing test the delivery and transfer incarnations agree with each other AND happen to be the intended recipient's, so the consistency-only verification is invisible to the suite as written. This is an instance of the campaign's catalogued pattern: the fixture cannot construct the state that distinguishes "consistent" from "correct".

issues.body:
Severity: P1. Repository: cao-conductor. Present in MERGED code at `dbd07398` (PR #161, cond-0426, M5b). This is a BILLING boundary, which the repository threat model does not waive.

DEFECT. The guard separating a free fixture run from a paid provider run fails OPEN on error paths. `conduct/commands/marshal.py:1145-1152` (guard), `:1154`, `:1164`.

The guard is realpath-equality between `--launcher` and the registry `HS_SCRIPT`, and it is evaluated ONLY when `harness_spec()` succeeds. A `KeyError` is caught and turned into `spec = None`, which disables BOTH guards:

    spec = None
    try:
        spec = marshal_probe.harness_spec(args.harness, repo_root=_repo_root())
    except KeyError:
        spec = None

THREE COOPERATIVE PATHS, ALL DEMONSTRATED.

(a) TYPO IN `--harness` WITH A REAL `--launcher`, NO `--provider-run`. The two arguments are independent and nothing cross-checks them once the registry lookup fails. Demonstrated with the free fixture harness standing in for a real one: `conduct marshal probe --harness codexx-typo --launcher <script> --fixtures ...` exits 0, runs the launcher, and stamps the result `local-fixture`. With a real launcher path this spends real provider quota with no indication anything is wrong.

Note the ASYMMETRY, which is the sharp part: the `--provider-run` direction of the same typo IS fail-closed (demonstrated: exit 1 with a clear refusal). The failure is exactly on the side that can bill silently.

(b) REGISTRY READ FAILURE. `harness_spec` also raises `KeyError` when the registry subprocess fails or times out (`marshal_probe.py:417-425`). A transient failure there - loaded machine, 30s subprocess timeout - silently converts a real-launcher run into a "fixture" run.

(c) THE BYTE-IDENTICAL DUPLICATE COPY. `launcher_fingerprint`'s own docstring (`marshal_probe.py:271-279`) records that every installed launcher exists TWICE on this installation: the `~/.claude/skills` symlink into skillshare, and a byte-identical copy in the custom-skills checkout. The guard compares RESOLVED paths, so naming the other copy of the same program defeats it. Demonstrated: copied the fixture to a registry path under a redirected `HEADLESS_SKILLS_ROOT`, then invoked a byte-identical copy at a different path with no `--provider-run`; exit 0, `evidence_class: local-fixture`, no receipt. With the real custom-skills copy of `codex-headless.sh` this is a paid run classified as fixture evidence.

STATE-INTEGRITY AND COST IMPACT. Unintended live provider launch across a billing boundary, with the run stamped `local-fixture`. The misclassification is at least in the SAFE direction for eligibility - nothing can be promoted from fixture evidence - so the cost is money and confusion rather than a false route. M5b is explicitly paid exact-build evidence, so silently converting a paid run into an unrecorded "fixture" also wastes the spend: no receipt is written, and the matrix must be paid for again.

FIX DIRECTION. Fail closed: `spec is None` should be an error for ANY invocation, not a silent "fixture". For (c), consider comparing on content digest rather than resolved path, since `launcher_fingerprint` already computes one and the duplicate-copy fact is already documented in that module.

NOTE ON THE FLEXIBILITY LENS. `AGENTS.md` now requires that guardrails not make the flow brittle, and prefers adapt or degrade over refuse. That lens does not soften this one. The explicit carve-out in the threat model names provider billing as a boundary that is applied as written, and the concrete bad transition here - spending the operator's money without their intent - is exactly the kind a guardrail is for. Refusing an ambiguous invocation is cheap, immediately diagnosable, and trivially recoverable by correcting the argument.

issues.body:
Severity: P2. Repository: cao-conductor. Present in MERGED code at `dbd07398` (PR #161, cond-0426, M5b).

DEFECT. A transient failure on the RESUME leg is recorded as a containment ANSWER, and `record()` replaces by design, so it destroys a good receipt.

`conduct/lib/marshal_probe.py:1049-1052` (resume `launcher_error` becomes a cell FAIL); `conduct/commands/marshal.py:1268-1281` (a receipt is recorded whenever `result["refusal"] is None`).

The CLI correctly refuses to record a receipt when the WHOLE run refuses - "A refusal is not an answer", `marshal.py:1268-1277`. But a launcher error on the resume leg (a timeout, a missing handle block, a wedged launch) does not set `result["refusal"]`. It becomes a FAIL on `exact-session-resume`, which is a GATING cell, so the run scores `uncontained` and IS recorded.

COOPERATIVE FAILURE SEQUENCE. A route with a good `contained` receipt is re-probed as a routine refresh. The launch leg succeeds and bills. The resume leg hits a transient provider or machine hiccup. The good receipt is overwritten with a transport-failure verdict. The route now reads `not-contained` and stays refused until someone pays for another full matrix.

DEMONSTRATED end to end in a temp store: run 1 clean gives receipt `contained`; run 2 identical except the resume leg returns `launcher_error` (simulated timeout) gives `refusal: None`, containment `uncontained`, and the CLI logic records it; `receipt_for` then reads `uncontained` and `evaluate` returns `not-contained`.

STATE-INTEGRITY IMPACT. "We measured and it failed" and "the measurement itself failed partway" become indistinguishable in the DURABLE record. That is precisely the confusion the refusal guard was built to prevent, reproduced one level down. The cost is a wrongly-refused route plus a paid re-run to recover.

The session-capture cell has the same shape: no captured session id means resume is never attempted, which is MISSING, which is an integrity failure on a gating cell, which scores `uncontained` and is recorded.

FIX DIRECTION. A transport failure on any leg should propagate as a refusal rather than as a cell verdict, so the existing "a refusal is not an answer" guard covers it. At minimum, a leg-level `launcher_error` must not be allowed to overwrite an existing receipt.

NOTE ON THE FLEXIBILITY LENS. This is the lens arguing FOR a change, not against one: today a small transient hiccup destroys durable evidence and costs real money to rebuild. Preferring degrade over refuse here means keeping the prior receipt and reporting the measurement as incomplete, rather than recording a verdict the run never actually established.

issues.body:
Severity: P2. Repository: cao-conductor. Present in MERGED code at `dbd07398` (PR #161, cond-0426, M5b).

DEFECT. The paid probe measures the launcher's DEFAULT model and effort; the marshal deploys a DIFFERENT model and effort; and the receipt cannot say which one it measured.

`conduct/commands/marshal.py:1214-1223` builds the provider argv as layout dirs plus `--posture` only. `scripts/fire-marshal.sh:888-890` builds the real marshal argv as `--model "$HS_MODEL"`, `"$HS_EFFORT_FLAG" "${THINKING:-$HS_EFFORT}"`, `--posture`, `--dir`.

So the probe launches each harness on whatever the launcher defaults to, while the marshal launches the same harness with the registry `HS_MODEL`/`HS_EFFORT` - for example codex on `gpt-5.6-sol`, kimi on `k3` at max, claude on opus.

The receipt's `build` block pins launcher path, resolved path, digest, and `build_id` (`conduct/lib/marshal_receipts.py:115-122`). It records NO model and NO effort.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. The two cells this merge made load-bearing are exactly the two most sensitive to model choice: codeword recall across a resume, and instruction discipline on the denial cells. Those are capability-dependent behaviours, not mechanical ones.

COOPERATIVE FAILURE SEQUENCE. A launcher update, or a provider-side change to a default, shifts the launcher default model. The probe passes or fails on model X. The receipt is later read as evidence for a route that runs model Y. In one direction the operator pays for a matrix whose verdict does not describe the deployed configuration. In the other, a `contained` receipt certifies a weaker model than the one that will actually hold the marshal's authority.

STATE-INTEGRITY IMPACT. M5b exists to produce EXACT-BUILD evidence. This leaves a hole on the model axis, and nothing downstream can detect it, because the model is not in the receipt to compare. The evidence silently describes a configuration that was never deployed.

FIX DIRECTION. Either launch the probe with the registry `HS_MODEL`/`HS_EFFORT` so it measures what the marshal deploys, or record the resolved model and effort in the receipt `build` block so a reader can tell what was measured and refuse a mismatch. Recording it is the smaller change and is valuable even if the argv is also aligned. `--launcher-arg --model ... --launcher-arg ...` can close the argv side manually today, but nothing requires or records it.

issues.body:
## Symptom

One unreadable row in one source stops every successor operation in the whole
project. `successor_policy_registry.validate()` refuses the entire registry file
when any attempt carries a state this build does not recognise, so a
campaign-scoped record propagates a project-scoped refusal.

## Why the current shape is right, and where it overreaches

The whole-file refusal is deliberate and its stated reason is sound:

> A reader that quietly ignored a state it did not understand would compute a
> `fencing_claim` from the rows it did understand, i.e. it would report an
> unfenced source because it could not read the fence.

That is correct and must not change. Skipping an unreadable row while computing
a fence fails open, on the one surface where failing open means two workers in
one worktree. Any proposal to tolerate an unrecognised value per record and
reject only that record reintroduces exactly that hazard and should be refused.

The overreach is the blast radius, not the polarity. **Sources are independent
fences.** `sources` is keyed by source digest and each source's `fencing_claim`
is derived from its own attempts, so an unreadable row in source A says nothing
about source B. Refusing B because A is unreadable stops work whose correctness
never depended on the unreadable answer.

## Concrete exposure

`STATE_DISPOSED` is deliberately forward-incompatible: an older build refuses
the whole file on encountering it. That was accepted, with the deploy preflight
refusing a downgrade to a build that cannot read a released claim. The residual
case is narrower and still live: any future state, or a partially written row,
takes the entire project's successor subsystem down rather than the one source
it belongs to. In a campaign with 18 waiting tracks that is the difference
between one stuck lane and a stopped subsystem.

## Suggested direction

- Validate per source. Refuse the sources whose rows cannot be read, and return
  the readable sources normally, so callers addressing a different source
  proceed.
- Have the refusal name the source digest and the unreadable state, so the
  forward move is bounded to that source rather than the file.
- Keep the fail-closed polarity exactly as it is: within a source, an
  unrecognised state still refuses that source's fence computation entirely,
  and is never skipped.
- Narrow `deploy_inventory.disposed_claim_projects` in the same way, so a
  downgrade refuses only on the records a target build genuinely cannot
  represent rather than on the presence of any disposition anywhere in the
  project.

## Provenance

Raised by an independent guard-recalibration pass, which proposed the unsafe
per-record variant. The direction was right and the proposed fix was not; this
is the version that preserves the fence property.
issues.title: successor registry validation refuses the whole file for one unreadable source, stopping a project subsystem

issues.body:
## Symptom

Nothing detects a guard that can only ever refuse. A predicate whose permitting
branch is unreachable looks identical, from every existing signal, to a guard
whose targets all happened to be genuinely blocked: the suite is green, the
command exits non-zero with a well-formed refusal, and the operator reads a
correct-looking answer.

## Evidence that this class ships

`conduct successor dispose` was released, deployed, and used, and could not
return a releasing verdict for any target in any project. Bindingness was read
from the truthiness of an artifact-projection wrapper that `artifact_projection`
writes for every kind on every attempt, so `ledger` and `shim` answered
`unknown` unconditionally. The verb existed for one purpose and never once
performed it. Every unit around it passed, and the composition was never
asserted.

Separately, managed recovery verified for 0 of 229 journaled runs on this host.
Each individual refusal was well formed and every one of them was wrong.

Both are the same shape: a guard firing at 100% with nobody counting.

## Why the existing signals miss it

- A refusal-only test suite passes: it asserts the refusing branch, which works.
- CI passes: there is no failing case to fail.
- `conduct doctor` reports whether checks run, not what they conclude over time.
- The operator sees a refusal and reads it as a finding about the work, because
  that is what a refusal usually is.

## Suggested direction

Give `conduct doctor` a field-evidence check over recorded outcomes:

- Report any guard whose **releasing verdict has never been observed** across a
  campaign as inert, naming the guard and the number of refusals it issued.
  A guard that has refused many times and permitted zero times is either
  correct about a genuinely blocked fleet or defective, and the operator is the
  right party to tell those apart, but only if asked.
- Report any guard accumulating refusals past a declared threshold within one
  campaign as needing predicate review before the next campaign starts.
- Pair it with a merge-time requirement: a release verb ships only with a test
  that permits against a record the ordinary writer produced, not a fixture the
  test invented. The dispose census shipped inert because its fixture built
  `{"bound": True}`, a shape the production constructor never emits.

The design-time test and the field check catch different faults. The first
proves the permitting branch is reachable in principle; the second proves it is
reached in practice, and one night produced 229 firings of a single predicate
that was wrong on every record.

## Provenance

Raised by an independent guard-recalibration pass. Filed because the class is
demonstrated rather than hypothetical: two instances shipped this week, and
neither was found by a test.
issues.title: nothing detects a guard that can only ever refuse

issues.body:
## Symptom

A read timeout on the managed-launch POST crashes `conduct spawn` with an
unhandled Python traceback instead of returning the
`launch-response-loss-preserved` outcome that exists for exactly this case. The
durable run state is reconciled correctly, so nothing is corrupted, but the
caller receives a stack trace on stderr and no structured result, and has to
reconstruct the outcome by reading manifest files by hand.

## Mechanism

`CaoClient._request` wraps four failure shapes: `UnicodeDecodeError` and
`json.JSONDecodeError` into `CaoResponseUnreadable`, and
`urllib.error.HTTPError` and `urllib.error.URLError` into `CaoApiError`. A bare
`TimeoutError` is not among them.

`urlopen(req, timeout=...)` only surfaces a *connect* timeout as
`URLError(reason=timeout)`. A timeout while reading the response, after the
request has already been sent, propagates as a bare `TimeoutError` from the
socket layer.

The launch site catches `CaoApiError` only:

    try:
        launched = (client.launch_managed_generation_v2(reservation_id)
                    if protocol_route.is_v2
                    else client.launch_managed_generation(reservation_id))
    except CaoApiError as launch_error:
        ...            # reconcile by exact reservation read
                       # -> launch-response-loss-preserved

So the one exception that means *the request was sent and the answer never came
back* is the one that bypasses the handler written for that meaning.

The handler's own comment states the design intent, and it is right:

> The second surface has no reconcile endpoint, by design: a read of the exact
> reservation id is the whole recovery mechanism. It reports the state a lost
> response left behind without being able to create anything, where a blind
> re-POST could still be the call that starts a second pane.

A read timeout after the POST is the canonical case of a lost response. The
recovery is well designed and unreachable from its most likely trigger.

## Observed

2026-08-17T06:25:00Z, conductor 7b6aeaa, deploy attempt 50e56efd1705, task
`cond-0388-pr121-review-muse-native-r1`:

    File ".../conduct/commands/spawn.py", line 4622, in _run_managed
      launched = (client.launch_managed_generation_v2(reservation_id)
    File ".../conduct/lib/caoapi.py", line 226, in _request
      with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout or self.timeout) as resp:
    ...
    File ".../http/client.py", line 279, in _read_status
      line = self.fp.readline(_MAXLINE + 1)
    TimeoutError: timed out

Recorded state was `ambiguous-preserved / provider-launch-attempted` with
terminal `256aba37`, generation `dadcc835`, reservation
`9415fba5-22f7-4da5-879f-6f3b86c7d018`, protocol v2, no callback emitted. The
supervisor recovered by reading the run manifest and spawn-delivery files
directly and then running `conduct spawn --recover`, which is correct behaviour
against a crash but is not the interface the command is supposed to present.

## Why it matters

1. The state this leaves behind is the most dangerous one in the launch path: a
   pane may exist and no callback proves it. That is precisely why
   `launch-response-loss-preserved` exists, and precisely when the operator
   most needs a typed outcome naming the next move.
2. An autonomous supervisor parses structured output. A traceback is not a
   result, so recovery depends on the supervisor independently knowing to read
   the durable files, which is a capability rather than a contract.
3. Every managed launch is exposed, on both protocol surfaces.

## Suggested direction

Wrap the timeout where every caller benefits rather than at one call site:
`_request` catches `TimeoutError` and raises `CaoApiError` naming the method and
path, with `safe_next_actions` pointing at the exact-reservation read. `OSError`
more broadly deserves the same treatment, since a connection reset carries the
same meaning as a read timeout.

Then confirm the launch site reaches `launch-response-loss-preserved` for a
timeout, with a test that raises `TimeoutError` from the client double. The
existing tests raise `CaoApiError`, which is why this gap is invisible to them.
issues.resolution: [ALREADY-FIXED] Commit 1dc59ea "cond-0460: a lost answer is typed, and an unadmitted bound row has a verb that closes it (#176)" — the commit directly before HEAD. conduct/lib/caoapi.py:131 `_RESPONSE_LOST_ERRORS = (OSError, http.client.HTTPException)` (TimeoutError and ConnectionResetError are OSError subclasses); :262-274 catches it AFTER the URLError clause and raises CaoResponseLost; :138 CaoResponseLost subclasses CaoApiError, so the existing handler at conduct/commands/spawn.py:4637 `except CaoApiError as launch_error:` now receives it and reaches launch-response-loss-preserved at :4650. Tests: tests/test_spawn.py:2333 test_a_transport_lost_launch_answer_reaches_its_recovery_rather_than_a_traceback drives a real socket close on POST /launch; `python3 -m unittest tests.test_caoapi` -> Ran 31 tests, OK. | The exact fix the issue asked for, at the level it asked for it: wrapped in `_request` so all 44 client methods benefit, with the ordering constraint made explicit (URLError first, because it is itself an OSError and would otherwise relabel a request that never left the machine as one the server may have carried out). status_code stays None so every downstream branch reads it as "no considered answer" rather than licensing a resend. The event that used to bypass the handler is now the canonical input to it. | Vetted 2026-08-17 against origin/main 1f0b8a6 in an 8-agent sweep of all 64 open P0/P1 issues; every remove/soften recommendation was independently spot-checked against source.

issues.body:
Severity: P3. Repository: cli-agent-orchestrator. Not a product defect; a test-isolation defect that makes local verification unreliable and silently machine-dependent.

DEFECT. A large part of the test suite reads the OPERATOR's real `settings.json` rather than a fixture. On this machine the memory subsystem is disabled there, so those tests raise `MemoryDisabledError: memory subsystem is disabled. Set memory.enabled=true in settings.json to re-enable` and fail.

MEASURED. Running the exact CI invocation locally against UNMODIFIED fork main `1cfa6c04`:

    uv sync --all-extras --dev
    pytest test/ --ignore=test/providers/test_kiro_cli_integration.py --ignore=test/e2e -m "not e2e"

gives `402 failed, 10107 passed, 9 errors`, against `4 failed, 10508 passed` for the same commit in hosted CI. The ~398 extra failures are entirely the memory / wiki / scoring / operation-journal / restore-contract cluster. CI's clean environment has no operator settings to read, so it never hits this.

WHY IT MATTERS. Live operator configuration is an undeclared input to the suite:

- A local total is never comparable to a CI total, and never comparable between two machines, so the ordinary "did I break anything" check silently stops working locally.
- A local run can be perturbed by editing `settings.json`, which no test declares as an input and no failure message attributes.
- With ~400 pre-existing failures locally, a genuine new failure is easy to miss by eye. Only a failure-ID set comparison is trustworthy, which is materially more work than reading a totals line.
- It cost real time twice in one session. The first diagnosis attributed the discrepancy to a stale worktree venv or missing extras, which was wrong; the real cause was only established when someone ran the exact CI invocation against an unmodified base.

COOPERATIVE FAILURE SEQUENCE. An implementer verifies a change locally, sees ~400 failures, cannot tell which are theirs, and either reports a number that means nothing or spends the effort to build id sets. In the worse direction, an implementer sees a familiar-looking large failure count, assumes it is the known environmental noise, and ships a real regression inside it.

FIX DIRECTION. Point the affected tests at a fixture settings file or an isolated config root (a monkeypatched settings path, or a `CAO_SETTINGS`-style env override honoured by the loader), so the suite declares its own configuration instead of inheriting the operator's. A narrower first step: make the memory-dependent tests skip explicitly with a stated reason when the subsystem is disabled, so the failure count stays honest even before isolation lands.

INTERIM GUIDANCE for anyone verifying locally in this repository: diff failure-ID SETS against the base commit. Do not compare totals, and do not treat the hosted-CI baseline (`4 failed, 10508 passed`, the four cond-0432 Claude-version assertions) as a local expectation.

PROVENANCE. Established by the cond-0439/0440/0441 batch implementer while proving no-regression for PR #129, after the coordinator's delegation brief had stated the CI baseline without labelling it CI-only. That batch proved no-regression by set comparison instead: 409 failing ids on a stashed base, 409 on the branch, identical, zero new and zero removed.
issues.resolution: fixed
issues.title: Local test runs read the operator real settings.json, so a local suite total is meaningless and machine-dependent

issues.body:
Severity: P2. Repositories: `cli-agent-orchestrator` (M6a detector) and `cao-conductor` (M8 effect). Scoping issue, opened on operator direction that automated detection of these API errors be accounted for either inside the M6a/M8 work or as a follow-up.

## The environment fact that makes this a family rather than two one-offs

All provider traffic on this installation is routed through a **residential proxy**, which the operator reports is intermittently flaky. Both OpenAI/Codex and Anthropic/Claude requests traverse it.

That means a single root cause — proxy flakiness — surfaces as **two different provider-shaped error screens**. The M6a corpus and its executing allowlist are organised per provider, so the same underlying condition would otherwise be gated, evidenced, and allowlisted twice, on two independent evidence-gate passes, while sharing one cause and one correct response.

It also means these errors are **recurrent and environment-driven**, not rare provider outages. That changes the cost/benefit of automation sharply in favour of doing it, and it changes the budget analysis below.

## What the plan already covers, and what it does not

Layer 0 exists: M6a detects provider terminal errors in the fork and emits `recovery_evidence` (detector/version/pattern, closed `turn_state`, closed `recovery_action`, bounded raw text plus digest, confidence/reason/signals); M6b projects it through the conductor without dropping fields. Both are merged and dark.

Layer 1's recognized-error cadence is M8, which is remaining and depends on M3-F, M6a, M6b, and all M7 stages. Its only initial action is one static `Continue your current task.` submission to the exact current, live, admitted native-TUI generation, for a provider-error occurrence with `turn_state=terminal` and `recovery_action=nudge`.

M6a's initial executing allowlist is deliberately narrow: the locally proven Claude connection-closed exact line to terminal/nudge; an observed retry banner to self-retrying/ignore; an anchored generic API error to unknown and layer 2. **Codex/OpenAI is not in it.** The plan requires other providers to pass the targeted M6a evidence gate — local or source-derived reproductions first, documentation only where the behaviour cannot be exercised safely, and an independent harness or reviewer challenging the result.

So the gap is not the mechanism. It is (a) corpus coverage for the OpenAI surface, and (b) the two design consequences below, which follow from the cause being shared infrastructure rather than a provider.

## Design consequence 1 — a proxy error is not a provider outage, and the evidence should not say it is

`recovery_evidence` carries provider and version. If a proxy-induced transport failure is classified as a provider error, every downstream reader — marshal evidence, recovery attribution, and any later reliability judgement about a route — misattributes cause to the provider. On this installation that would systematically defame whichever provider happened to be mid-request when the proxy hiccupped, and it would corrupt exactly the evidence M5b-style route decisions are meant to rest on.

Wanted: a signal distinguishing a transport-layer failure reaching the provider from a failure reported by the provider. The `signals` and `reason` fields already exist to carry it; what is missing is the classification.

## Design consequence 2 — the shared recovery budget interacts badly with a flaky link

M8-A owns an at-most-three-inputs-in-ninety-minutes policy keyed by `(CAO session, stable agent_id, task occurrence)`. A flaky proxy can plausibly produce more than three interruptions in ninety minutes on one occurrence. If transport-induced nudges consume the same budget as genuine provider-error nudges, a bad proxy hour exhausts the budget and the worker parks for the remainder of the window — the automation then makes a recoverable condition durable, which is the opposite of its purpose.

Two candidate resolutions, and the choice is a real one:

1. Classify self-healing transport blips as `self-retrying`/ignore so they consume no budget at all, leaning on the provider's own retry. This is the cheapest and matches the existing retry-banner precedent, but it requires knowing which blips self-heal.
2. Give transport-class recovery a separate budget from provider-error recovery, on the grounds that they have different expected frequencies and different costs of being wrong.

Neither should be chosen without the corpus in hand, which is why this is scoping rather than a fix.

## The operator's own standing constraint applies with full force here

The authoritative ruling recorded on the OpenAI `Additional safety checks` screen is that the appearance of a transient is **not** actionable: default handling is passive wait with no answer, no recovery-budget consumption, no deadman nudge, and no human-blocker alert, and escalation requires a separately specified timeout plus durable proof the transient failed to resolve.

A flaky proxy produces exactly the class of error most likely to self-resolve on the next request. So the detector must be able to say "the provider is retrying, do nothing" and be right, or the automation will spend budget interrupting turns that were about to recover on their own. Two closed incidents show the cost of getting the timing wrong: a stale deadman delivered after its obligation closed reactivated a completed worker and wasted quota, and queued nudges sat unconsumed in a Kimi composer while the turn continued past its boundary.

## What is needed next, and what is blocking

**Blocked on evidence, not on design.** The load-bearing input is the **exact anchored literal text** of each error surface, because M6a matches on anchored patterns and explicitly must not guess. Required, and not yet captured:

- the Codex/OpenAI error line or screen, verbatim;
- the Claude Code error line or screen, verbatim;
- for each: whether the harness self-retried and recovered without intervention, and whether the turn was terminally dead or resumed.

The operator observed both surfaces but the screenshots did not reach the session, so the literal text is still outstanding. Capturing it while the condition recurs is the slow part of the M6a evidence gate; the classification work is cheap once the anchors exist.

Related: the open P2 "Claude connection-closed turns return idle without a typed recovery wake" covers the Anthropic surface's missing typed wake and should be read alongside this. M6a is `cond-0307` (merged), M6b is `cond-0214` (merged), M8 is the remaining layer-1 recognized-error cadence.

issues.body:
Severity: P2. Repository: `cao-conductor`. A handoff obligation created by cond-0444, raised by the independent review of PR #173. Filing it so cond-0444 does not silently reopen at read time.

## What cond-0444 fixed, and the half it cannot reach

cond-0444 closed the gap where the M5b probe measured the launcher's DEFAULT model while the marshal deployed the registry's `HS_MODEL`/`HS_EFFORT`, and the receipt recorded neither. PR #173 aligns the probe argv to the registry values and records `build.model` and `build.effort` in the receipt, so a receipt now states the configuration the probe actually measured.

That closes the WRITE side. The READ side is still open, and it is not closable in the probe.

## The residual: an operator override diverges from what the receipt certifies

`scripts/fire-marshal.sh:888-889` deploys `--model "$HS_MODEL"`, but `HS_MODEL` is replaced by `MODEL_FORCED` when the operator passes `--model` (`:236-261`, `:802`), and effort is `"${THINKING:-$HS_EFFORT}"`. The probe always measures, and the receipt always records, the REGISTRY values. So an operator override on the marshal side produces a deployed configuration the receipt never measured, on both axes.

COOPERATIVE FAILURE SEQUENCE. The operator runs the paid probe matrix and gets a receipt reading codex / `gpt-5.6-sol` / `xhigh` / contained. Later, during a long incident and to conserve quota, they launch the marshal with `--model codex/gpt-5.6-sol-low` or `--thinking low`. The marshal deploys a weaker configuration than the receipt certifies, on exactly the two cells this milestone made load-bearing: codeword recall across a resume, and instruction discipline on the denial cells. Nothing downstream detects it, because nothing compares.

This sequence is not hypothetical for this operator: conserving quota by dropping to a cheaper model or a lower effort during an incident is ordinary practice here, which is what makes the read-side comparison worth building rather than assuming.

WHY IT IS BOUNDED TODAY. The override is an explicit operator action and the marshal prints it ("explicit --model override"). More importantly, `marshal_receipts.evaluate` has ZERO production callers — receipts are written by `conduct/commands/marshal.py` and read only by tests, `fire-marshal.sh` does not touch the store, and eligibility is explicitly deferred to M5c (`conduct/lib/marshal_receipts.py:20-25`). So there is no consumer yet to be silently misled.

WHY IT WAS CORRECTLY NOT FIXED IN PR #173. Adding an expected-model parameter to `evaluate` would have been a check nothing calls — unreachable code, the half-built shape `AGENTS.md` forbids. Recording the model and effort is different in kind: a receipt is an evidence document whose reader is named in the design. The write side belongs to cond-0444; the comparison belongs here.

## The obligation

When M5c builds the eligibility read, it must compare the receipt against the configuration `fire-marshal.sh` will ACTUALLY launch, overrides included, on BOTH the model and the effort axis. Either:

- compare against the resolved deployment configuration rather than the registry defaults, so an override that the receipt does not cover is visible; or
- have `fire-marshal.sh` refuse, or loudly mark, an override the receipt does not cover.

Whichever is chosen, "the receipt says contained" must not be readable as "this launch is contained" when the launch differs from what was measured.

NOTE ON SCOPE, from the same review: the implementer flagged the `THINKING` effort override but not the model override, which travels the identical `MODEL_FORCED` path. Both axes are in scope here; fixing only effort would leave the more consequential half open.

Related: cond-0444 (write side, PR #173), cond-0443 (same PR), cond-0426 (M5b probe adapter).

issues.body:
Deploying the conductor requires an exact operator disposition for every parked v1 retained track installation-wide, and the whole disposition file is invalidated whenever ANY part of the inventory changes. With more than one live campaign this is a race the operator loses: the approval goes stale before it can be spent.

Reproduced 2026-08-17. `conduct deploy --repo /Users/colin/Projects/cao-conductor --inventory-retained-v1` exits 1 with 15 parked v1 tracks spanning THREE unrelated campaigns:

- aegix-mobile-phase0-renewal (2)
- dnd-scheduler (6)
- p1-closure (7)

So a conductor deploy needed by the p1-closure campaign is gated on the operator individually disposing of parked workers in the Aegix mobile and D&D scheduler campaigns. Ordinary activity in ANY of those three then invalidates the approval for all fifteen.

That is what happened: the p1-closure supervisor merged PR #121 at exact head 509e0ef (merge commit 47b90150), advanced the deployment source to origin/main, and was then held. The previously approved file
/Users/colin/.local/state/cao-conductor/retained-v1-dispositions-cond0431-e7f44b5.json
was rejected as stale against the fresh inventory. The supervisor acted correctly: it refused to reuse or fabricate the stale approval and parked. Deployment and final implementer retirement have been held since.

## Where it comes from

`conduct/lib/deploy_inventory.py:453`

    if dispositions.get("inventory_sha256") != inventory["inventory_sha256"]:
        raise InventoryHold("the disposition file was written against a different inventory; re-run the read-only inventory and re-approve")

`inventory_sha256` is computed at :387 over the ENTIRE inventory document. Any change anywhere in it - including rows for campaigns whose tracks the operator already disposed of, and fields no disposition depends on - discards all fifteen approvals at once.

## Why that comparison is not the thing protecting anything

`validate_dispositions` already enforces every safety property the file needs, per track:

- :473 a parked track with no disposition holds ("missing")
- :476 a disposition for a track that is no longer parked holds ("extra")
- :482 `track_sha256` must equal that track's CURRENT digest
- :485 `execution_mode_migration_sha256` must match
- :491-:501 classification/disposition pairing is validated per row

The per-track digest at :482 is what makes a decision non-stale: it refuses precisely when the thing the operator looked at has changed. The whole-document comparison at :453 adds no safety property those checks do not already provide. What it adds is blast radius - it converts "this one track moved" into "every approval is void".

This is the same shape as cond-0457 (registry validation refuses the whole file for one bad record) and as the source-proof staleness defect in the transport scope (whole deploy receipt compared when only five fields are bound). Narrow the compared identity; keep the fail-closed polarity exactly as it is.

## Proposed fix

1. Scope the compared identity to what the dispositions actually bind: the parked-v1 track set and their per-track digests, plus the project-roots identity. Do not compare the whole inventory document. Every per-track fence stays exactly as written.
2. Make dispositions accumulate rather than be re-rendered wholesale. Key a durable disposition record on (project, task_id, track_sha256) so an operator disposes of each track once, and a later deploy after unrelated drift asks only for the tracks that actually changed - O(changed) instead of O(all). The successor policy registry's append-only attempt model is the precedent.

Neither part lets a changed track through: :482 still refuses any disposition whose track digest moved, which is the whole point of the fence.

## Explicitly NOT proposed

Removing the operator gate. Deciding what becomes of a parked v1 worker across an execution-mode migration is reserved to the operator and must stay so. The defect is that the gate is unsatisfiable in a live multi-campaign installation, not that it exists.

## Verification

A fix must add a test where the inventory changes in a way that touches NO disposed track (e.g. a row in an unrelated campaign) and assert the existing approval still validates; plus a test where a disposed track's own digest changes and assert it still refuses. Both must fail independently when the corresponding half is reverted - a single test would pass with the fence removed.

Every per-track fence the issue said was doing the real work is intact: missing :511-513, extra :514-516, track_sha256 :520-521, execution_mode_migration_sha256 :522-527, classification/disposition pairing :528-539. The companion half (cond-0469, the inventory printing its digests without a disposition file) landed in the same commit. | The false-stale refusal this issue describes cannot occur on current main: a row appearing in an unrelated campaign moves inventory_sha256 and no longer voids anything, while a disposed track whose own digest moved still refuses at :520. The operator gate itself was explicitly kept, as the issue asked. The open questions the comments raise (whether approved_by 'external-runtime-steward-cond0431-cutover' represents the operator's own decision; the deliberately unbuilt revoke verb) are separate decisions already recorded, not reasons to keep this row open. | Vetted 2026-08-17 against origin/main 1f0b8a6 in an 8-agent sweep of all 64 open P0/P1 issues; every remove/soften recommendation was independently spot-checked against source.
