issues.body:
Severity: P2. Repository: `cli-agent-orchestrator`. Found while implementing cond-0485.

## The finding

cond-0485 publishes a restore contract at teardown, which was the missing producer that made `has_exact_resume_identity` and `cohort_resume._has_resume_identity` return False for every agent. That half is fixed.

**It does not make resurrection work end to end, and it was reported as partial rather than as the unblock.**

The contract published at teardown carries `executable: unavailable`, because the executable identity — along with model, effort, and profile/provider-home material — **is never persisted at launch**. It cannot be recovered at teardown: the pane is dead and no durable record holds it.

`exact_executor._fact_refusal` hard-requires a present executable fact. So it now refuses on the *missing* fact, before the digest comparison is even reached.

## What cond-0485 did and did not move

| gate | before | after cond-0485 |
|---|---|---|
| `has_exact_resume_identity` | False for every agent | passes for managed agents |
| `cohort_resume._has_resume_identity` | `unresumable` for every member | members get exact-restore requests |
| `exact_executor._fact_refusal` | never reached | **refuses: executable fact unavailable** |

So fleet Stop is reversible at the roster and journal gates, and still not reversible end to end.

## What is missing

**Persist the launch facts at launch.** At minimum the executable identity; also model, effort, and the profile/provider-home material the contract declares. These are known at launch and knowable nowhere else afterwards.

Unmanaged launches additionally have no durable `working_directory`, which is hard-required, so they stay on the plain retirement path and remain unresurrectable — acceptable for now, but it should be a stated limitation rather than a silent one.

## Ordering note

This is the second of two producers. It is also the point at which the auto-update digest pin becomes the live gate: once the executable fact is present, `_fact_refusal` compares a digest recorded at launch against the binary on disk at resume, and every one of these CLIs auto-updates in place. Muse updated twice in a single session on 2026-08-17.

So this issue and the digest-pin demotion should land together or in quick succession, or resurrection will move from "refused, no executable fact" straight to "refused, digest differs" without ever working.

## Acceptance criterion

Not "the facts are written." An agent launched, retired, and resurrected after a provider auto-update must come back on its preserved native session — or must refuse for a reason that is about the resume being illegal, never about bookkeeping nobody recorded.
issues.resolution: Triage 2026-08-21 vs vision + main 13bcdcc: Obsolete — teardown executable unavailable premise dissolved; cond-0485 design publishes restore contract at BIND not teardown (f0dc62ee no production caller). Half-built mis-located. Superseded by cond-0485 BIND implementation. If BIND omits executable, refile narrowly.
issues.title: launch facts are never persisted, so a teardown-published restore contract carries executable unavailable and resurrection still refuses

issues.body:
Severity: P2. Repository: `cli-agent-orchestrator`. Found by the operator, verified end to end on the Mac mini against Muse 0.2.1-R1215.1.

Supersedes the Muse half of the identity problem. Muse is currently the weakest of the four providers on session identity — its id is scraped from the rendered `/status` panel (`muse_native_status.py:233`, `fields["Session:"]`), which is the same fragility class as composer-hint parsing and breaks on any layout change.

**There is a zero-cost, fully deterministic pre-turn mint, and it is stronger than what Codex or Kimi have.**

## The technique

```bash
uuid=$(muse exec --provider echo --json "." | head -1 | jq -r '.stream.id')
muse --provider meta resume "$uuid"     # launch the TUI on that exact session
```

Verified on this machine:

- `muse exec --provider echo --json` emits JSONL on stdout where **every record carries the full session UUID** in `.stream.id` — present on **line 1**, before any output. Extracted `82d31f4a-8ac5-45ec-a4a8-ddd9adf9e46d`, confirmed canonical, and confirmed the session directory `~/.local/share/muse/sessions/2026/08/18/<uuid>/` was created.
- `--provider echo` is **local and deterministic**: no network, no API key, no billing. The response is canned. Session count incremented, exit 0.
- `muse resume --help` states root options including `--provider` "may appear on either side of `resume`", so a session minted under `echo` can be resumed under `meta`. That is what closes the loop: free mint, real provider on resume.

## Why this is better than the alternatives

| provider | mint mechanism | cost |
|---|---|---|
| Codex | app-server `thread/start` + `thread/name/set` | spawns a process, real protocol exchange |
| Kimi | ACP `session/new` | a short ACP conversation |
| Muse **today** | scrape the rendered `/status` panel | free, but parses a human UI |
| Muse **proposed** | `exec --provider echo --json`, read `.stream.id` | free, machine-readable, no UI |

It is the only one of the four where the id arrives as a structured field on stdout rather than from a protocol handshake or a rendered surface.

## What it replaces, and what it does not

**Replaces:** `muse_native_status.py`'s `/status` panel scrape as the identity source, and with it Muse's dependence on the header layout surviving a release. The panel scrape can stay as a cross-check.

**Does not replace:** the profile-carrier cell (base instructions injection, `TBH_EVAL_APPEND_SYSTEM_PROMPT_FILE`), which is a separate concern with its own echo-provider probe already designed. Nor does it address `_fact_refusal`'s executable digest pin.

## Open questions to establish before implementing

1. **Does the resumed session inherit anything unwanted from the echo mint?** The mint records one turn with a canned response. Does that pollute the resumed context, and if so is there a prompt that mints while contributing nothing? An empty or single-character prompt was used here (`"."`).
2. **Does the profile carrier survive the mint-then-resume boundary?** The carrier injects base instructions via an env-addressed file; confirm the resumed session carries them, since that is exactly the property the carrier cell exists to guarantee.
3. **Concurrency.** Multiple agents minting simultaneously is safe under this technique because each `exec` returns its own id on its own stdout — no directory globbing, no newest-by-mtime race. Confirm no shared lock serialises them.
4. **The date-partitioned path** (`sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/`) matters only for filesystem lookup, which this technique avoids. Anything that does glob the store must handle a launch crossing midnight.

## Acceptance criterion

A Muse worker's native session id is known before any task bytes reach its pane, obtained without reading a rendered surface, and an exact resume returns to that same session. No `/status` parse on the identity path.
issues.title: Muse has a zero-cost deterministic pre-turn session mint via exec --provider echo --json, replacing the /status panel scrape

issues.body:
Severity: P2. Repository: `cli-agent-orchestrator`. Operator-confirmed on Muse 0.2.1-R1215.1.

## Ground truth, observed tier

**The operator drove the installed Muse TUI and confirmed `Ctrl+J` inserts a newline.** That is `observed` evidence — the strongest tier — and it establishes that Muse multi-line delivery is currently refused for a reason that is about our reading technique, not about the capability.

They also noted `ctrl+j` does **not** appear in Muse's TUI help. The binary explains why: the help run advertises one binding, while the binding table carries three.

## What actually broke

cond-0481 derives the composer newline keystroke from the installed bundle. Muse derivation returns `None` on 0.2.1 because `installed_bundle_facts._extract` requires the key run and the human-readable description to be byte-adjacent, and 0.2.1 moved the descriptions into a separate table ~1339 bytes away.

The **binding table itself survived the update intact**. Verified in `/Users/colin/.local/bin/muse-bin-0.2.1-R1215.1`:

```
composer submit enter newline shift+enter ctrl+j ctrl+m queue alt+enter
```

Counts: `ctrl+j` 4, `ctrl+m` 4, `shift+enter` 5, `newline` 30.

So `newline` carries three bindings and the description table is a localized UI label. **Anchor on the key table; it is the stronger evidence.**

## The hazard, and why this is not a regex widening

`ctrl+m` **is** carriage return. Sent through tmux it is Enter — submit. An extractor that anchored on "the first binding after `newline`", or matched greedily across the concatenated run, could select `shift+enter` (unreliable through tmux, which is why `C-j` is the chosen form elsewhere) or `ctrl+m` (**submits mid-message**, the exact failure the refusal exists to prevent).

The bindings are concatenated with no separators, so a tokenizer must recognise known key-spec forms rather than split on a delimiter.

**Match `ctrl+j` as an exact token within the run anchored to `newline`.** Do not generalise to "extract the binding."

## Scope

- Re-fit the Muse arm of `installed_bundle_facts._extract` to anchor on the key run rather than key+description adjacency.
- Emit `C-j` only when `ctrl+j` is found inside the `newline` binding run — never a positionally-inferred key.
- Keep the existing refusal when the run does not read.
- Do **not** change the Claude or Kimi arms; both derive correctly today.
- The two tables are 1339 bytes apart, well inside the existing 64 KiB overlap window, so no new read strategy is required.

## Validation available

Unusually, ground truth exists: `C-j` is operator-confirmed working on the installed build. A derivation that returns anything other than `C-j` for 0.2.1-R1215.1 is measurably wrong, and one that returns `C-j` is measurably right. Pin that.

Also worth recording the operator's live confirmation as `observed` evidence alongside the derived value, since the two agree — that is the four-forms situation §1 of the policy describes, and it is the first time this build has had one.

## Why it matters

Muse multi-line operator messages, steer text, and any multi-line delivery are refused today. This is the one of the four harnesses where the refusal is known to be unnecessary.
issues.title: Muse newline derivation must anchor on the binding table, not key+description adjacency; ctrl+j is operator-confirmed working on 0.2.1

issues.body:
agy merged (colindmurray/cli-agent-orchestrator#137) as an **identity-and-resume-only** provider. Its native identity capture is the strongest of any provider we support — `agy -p <prompt> --output-format json` returns `conversation_id`, so the id is minted deterministically before the TUI starts and the pane binds `--conversation <uuid>` to that exact id. What is missing is the control plane.

## Present state

- `provider_controls` has **no antigravity row** in its capability registry (`_codex_entry` / `_kimi_entry` / `_claude_entry`), and no entry in `_SHORT_NAME_FOR_WIRE`. `_build_supports_operator_message` therefore returns `False` at the `short is None` branch, so agy advertises **no `operator_message` block at all** — nor steer chords, nor image.
- There is **no `antigravity_native_control.py`**, so there is no `_PROVEN_COMPOSER_NEWLINE`-equivalent for agy even if a registry row existed.
- agy is **not** in `managed_launch_v2.NATIVE_TUI_PROVIDERS` or `_PINNED_PROVIDER`.

agy is nonetheless **driveable today** through the generic tmux bracketed-paste sink, which needs no composer table. This issue is about giving it the same first-class control surface the other four have, not about making it usable at all.

## The operator-confirmed fact this is waiting on

`ctrl+j` inserts a newline in an agy chat — confirmed live by the operator on `1.1.14`. That is the missing ingredient for a composer plan.

**Record it at the evidence tier it actually has.** It is `observed` (a live operator observation on a named build), not bundle-derived: agy is a compiled Go binary and `installed_bundle_facts` cannot honestly derive a keybinding from it, nor version-bind such a read. Do not invent a bundle needle for it.

**Hazard, from the Muse re-fit:** if any extractor is ever written, match `ctrl+j` as an exact token. `ctrl+m` IS carriage return, and through tmux would submit mid-message.

## Half-built surface to resolve in the same change

`native_tui_launch._ARGV_BINDERS` gained an `antigravity_cli` entry (`_antigravity_argv` / `_antigravity_binds_exactly`), but `NATIVE_TUI_PROVIDERS` omits agy, so **nothing can reach that binder**. Per AGENTS.md this is the half-built shape: either wire agy into the native-TUI path so the binder is reachable, or delete the binder. Do not leave a builder nothing dispatches to.

Two smaller notes on that binder if it is kept:
- `_antigravity_argv` ignores its `launch_kind` parameter, unlike every other provider's builder. Confirm that is correct for a mint-then-resume design rather than a latent defect.
- It does not route through `provider_contracts.validate_resume_argv`, which does have an antigravity branch accepting `--conversation <uuid>` (verified: real conversation ids on disk are canonical lowercase UUIDs, so the validator's requirement holds).

## Acceptance

- A multi-line operator message reaches an agy pane through the same seam the other providers use, with `C-j` recorded as `observed` on `1.1.14` and a settle value that is a measured floor rather than a null default.
- `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS[antigravity]` stays **empty** and no new capability allowlist is introduced — agy is deliberately unpinned (see #137; it auto-updated 1.1.13 -> 1.1.14 mid-merge, which is why).
- Either the argv binder is reachable, or it is gone.

## Not part of this

The cohort-resume `unresumable` outcome for agy members is **not** agy-specific — `_has_resume_identity` requires `restore_contract_id`/`restore_contract_digest`, which no production writer publishes for ANY provider. That is cond-0485, not this.

issues.body:
A new non-nullable column with no server_default was added to `task_occurrence_handoffs`, which SQLite cannot ADD COLUMN to an existing table. Every managed write on an upgraded installation is then refused as `handoff-hold-undecidable` until the table is rebuilt by hand.

## Observed on the live installation 2026-08-18

Upgrading the fork from a build predating PR #132 to `a299bf62` produced, at `init_db()`:

    ERROR - task-occurrence handoff column reconcile left this store a column short:
    task_occurrence_handoffs on this store is missing ['donor_revision'], which SQLite
    cannot ADD COLUMN to a populated table. Make the column nullable, give it a
    server_default, or rebuild the table explicitly.. init_db() continues because a
    typed refusal beats a dead installation, but every managed write on this store
    will be refused as handoff-hold-undecidable until the table is rebuilt

Consequence, reproduced immediately after: `conduct control-input --project p1-closure --terminal 7b1a724b --command /compact --enter` returned exit 60, `outcome: conflict`, `state: refused`, reason `handoff-hold-undecidable`, transport all false. No control input could be delivered to any terminal on the installation.

Note the table was **empty** - 0 rows - and the migration still could not add the column. The refusal is not about protecting data; it is about the column shape.

## What is right about the current behaviour

The degraded state is loud and typed rather than silent, and `init_db()` deliberately continues on the principle that a typed refusal beats a dead installation. The error names three remedies. None of that should change.

## What is wrong

The migration ships a column SQLite cannot append, so the degradation is not an edge case - it is the *guaranteed* outcome of upgrading any installation whose `task_occurrence_handoffs` table already exists. The remedy it names ("rebuild the table explicitly") is a manual database operation with no supported command behind it, on a table an operator has no reason to know about.

`_reconcile_columns_from_model` is explicitly built to append columns to older stores. A column it cannot append defeats the mechanism it was written for, at the one moment that mechanism exists to cover.

## Fix

Make `donor_revision` appendable: nullable, or carrying a `server_default`. The model is the authority for the shape, and the error message already prescribes exactly this. Then a future column of the same shape cannot reintroduce the failure.

Two things worth adding alongside:

1. A build-time check that every column in a model reconciled by `_reconcile_columns_from_model` is appendable - nullable or defaulted. `test_no_column_added_after_m3e_is_beyond_alter_table` gates a related shape already; this is its sibling. Without it the next non-appendable column repeats this exactly.
2. A supported rebuild path, so "rebuild the table explicitly" is a command rather than manual SQL. Whoever hits this on an upgrade should not need to open the database.

## Repair applied here, recorded for reproducibility

The table was empty, so it was backed up (`db/cli-agent-orchestrator.db.bak-20260818-donor-revision`), dropped, and recreated by the next `init_db()` during a deploy bounce. Verified after: the table exists with 28 columns including `donor_revision`, the log carries no further "column short" error, and `conduct control-input` to the previously blocked terminal returned `ok: true`, `state: posted`, transport `enter_sent/posted/text_sent` all true.

This repair is only safe because the table was empty. An installation with rows would need the copy-into-new-table rebuild that SQLite requires, which is precisely why a supported path matters.

Related: cond-0413, whose fix is what surfaced this - once the assert stopped crashing control input, the next refusal in line became visible.
issues.resolution: Fork PR #144 merged as part of the fork's main line; all 12 hosted checks green including AG-UI demo (shift-left recording), which had been the one check under suspicion. donor_revision is now appendable and a supported rebuild path exists. Left as resolved rather than closed: the original report was an observed live outage, so a verifier should confirm managed writes are accepted on a real upgraded installation before closing.
issues.title: donor_revision cannot be ADD COLUMNed, so every upgraded store refuses managed writes until hand-rebuilt

issues.body:
Two lanes landing in the same window each change supervisor resolution in
`conduct/commands/_common.py`. Both are correct alone; composed, the gate
answer routes to the pane `conduct revive` existed to replace.

## The two halves

**Supervisor-lifecycle lane** (`fix/supervisor-lifecycle-recovery`) taught
`resolve_supervisor_terminal` that a local revival succession record demotes a
server-live predecessor. Its own comment states the premise: after a revive of
a wedged pane, "the server still reports the old pane live", so without the
filter every downstream resolver deadlocks on `multiple-live-supervisors`.

**Gate-response lane** (`feat/gate-response-conversation`) added
`resolve_gate_response_target`, a two-rung ladder. Rung 1
(`recorded-requester`) returns the terminal that filed the gate request when
`live_terminal_in_session` says it is still live. Rung 2 (`profile-fallback`)
resolves the live profile holder instead, and its docstring says why that rung
is policy rather than a refusal: "revival and handoff between request and
answer are ordinary".

## The composition

`live_terminal_in_session` decides liveness from the server projection alone —
`lifecycle_is_adoptable(lifecycle_of_record(term))` — and consults no
retirement record. After a revive, the server still reports the retired
predecessor `live`. So rung 1 answers, returns the predecessor, and labels the
delivery `recorded-requester`: the rung documented as the exact one that
"cannot drift to a different supervisor".

Rung 2 never fires. The revive case is the main case rung 2 names, and the
composition makes it unreachable.

## Reproduction (executed against the composed tree)

Composed state: `origin/main` 9a1667e + `c69d510` + `740af69`, clean auto-merge
on `_common.py`. Fake session reports predecessor and successor both `live`
with the supervisor profile; a real retirement record written via
`retirement.record_supervisor_retirement` names the successor.

    resolve_supervisor_terminal      -> term-successor
    resolve_gate_response_target     -> term-predecessor  recorded-requester

The profile resolver the supervisor lane repaired gets the right answer. The
gate ladder never asks it.

## Sequence and impact

Supervisor A files a gate request; A wedges; the operator runs `conduct
revive`, creating successor B; the operator answers the gate. The verdict is
recorded correctly in the journal, so this is a lost delivery rather than
state corruption — but the answer is enqueued to a pane nobody is reading, and
the receipt reports the exact route, so nothing signals the miss. B learns the
gate was answered only by polling `conduct gate check`.

## Smallest correct fix

Have rung 1 decline a terminal that carries a recorded retirement whose
successor is itself live, so the ladder drops to rung 2.
`retirement.supervisor_retirement_for(psd, terminal_id)` is a direct lookup and
already exists. This adds no refusal and creates no new state: it makes an
existing fallback reachable in the case its own docstring names.

Note `resolve_gate_response_target` already receives `project_state_dir` and
forwards it to rung 2, so the fix needs no signature change.

## Why this is filed rather than fixed inside either branch

Neither candidate contains the defect. It exists only in the merged tree, so
the repair belongs after both land, and retro-editing a frozen reviewed
candidate would discard its review provenance.
issues.resolution: Triage 2026-08-21 vs vision + main 13bcdcc: Verified already-fixed on conductor main. Fix commit/proof cited in triage comment (see prior comment_id). Live file inspection (git log -S, grep) confirms defect absent. Vision: check now correctly scoped/closed; smallest check shipped. No further action. If re-observed, reopen with current file:line.
issues.title: A gate answer routes to the retired predecessor after a revive

issues.body:
*Surface:* dashboard communications viewer (`web/lib/safeMarkdown.ts`).

`MAX_MARKDOWN_RENDER_BYTES` is 512 KiB, a recorded §13.3 design decision. It is
a **byte budget used as a proxy for parse cost**, and PR 9C produced the first
measurement of how loose that proxy is: **512 KiB of dense emphasis measures
~62 s of synchronous parse** in the node rail. Content at or just under the
budget therefore passes the check and can still hang the tab, because the budget
gates on size before anything measures time.

PR 9C repaired the two defects this exposed — the module's prose claimed the
budgets "fail visibly rather than hang the tab", which was false and is now
corrected, and the check was re-running unmemoized on every render. Neither
repair changes the number, deliberately: moving a recorded design decision
inside a UI slice would be relitigating it rather than repairing a defect.

**The decision to revisit** is whether a byte budget is the right instrument at
all, now that there is evidence. Three shapes, in rough order of how much they
cost:

1. **Keep 512 KiB.** Dense-emphasis input is pathological rather than typical,
   and lowering the budget degrades every legitimate large report to defend
   against it. This is the current disposition.
2. **Lower the byte budget.** Blunt: it trades normal-content capability for
   worst-case protection, and the worst case is not bounded by any byte number
   — a smaller budget still has a pathological input.
3. **Bound the parse rather than the size.** Measures the thing actually cared
   about instead of a proxy, and is the only shape whose guarantee does not
   depend on the input's shape. Also the most work, and needs a real answer for
   what a partially-parsed document renders as.

Not urgent and not a merge blocker. Filed so the number is revisited against
this measurement rather than by feel, and so the next reader does not
rediscover the 62 s the hard way.

Threat-model note: the content is untrusted text, but the actors producing it
are cooperative local agents, so the realistic path here is a worker
accidentally emitting a pathological report, not an attack. Size the response
to that.

issues.body:
*Surface:* commit provenance in `cli-agent-orchestrator`.

Two commits on `origin/main` are authored `test <t@example.test>`:

- `fb113bcd` — "PR 9B: bounded communications catalog HTTP API"
- `860a4ba6` — "fix(communications-catalog): repair round 1 reviewer findings"

Every other commit in that history is authored `Colin Murray`. Both offenders
come from the same campaign lane, where a headless implementation agent
committed without a resolved git identity.

They are already merged (via PR #138), so the history is published and is not
worth rewriting for this. The value here is preventing recurrence: a later
reader auditing who wrote a given line gets a placeholder address, and a second
lane already cited these two commits as evidence that the placeholder was "this
fork's practice" — which it is not. Two instances of the same defect are not a
convention, and that misreading is exactly how a defect becomes a norm.

**Fix forward, not backward.** Every lane brief that spawns a headless
implementer should require the worker to commit through a shell where the
repository's identity resolution applies (a freshly-sourced login shell pinned
to the worktree), and to verify with `git log -1 --format='%an <%ae>'` before
handing the branch back. The coordinator should check authorship as part of
publishing, alongside the index digest and the gate counts — it was not checked
before #138 merged.

No production behaviour is affected.

issues.body:
*Surface:* `web/src/test` vocabulary firewall.

The guard asserts a module's source does not compare against conductor
vocabulary, via `expect(source).not.toMatch(/kind\s*[=!]==/)`. The pattern
allows only **whitespace** between `kind` and the operator, so
`annotation.kind === 'human-gate'` is caught while
`annotation['kind'] === 'human-gate'` is not.

Found during PR 9C, in the most instructive way available: an implementation
agent, asked to bring a module under the guard, rewrote three call sites from
dot to bracket notation. Semantically identical, and enough to pass. The module
would then have *appeared* covered while the guard had no power over it — so the
next genuinely wrong comparison written in brackets stays green, in a module the
suite reports as protected. That is worse than the module being openly excluded.

That instance was rejected and fixed at the source: the trigger was a false
positive (a local `DetailFailure.kind` discriminant carrying no conductor
vocabulary), so the colliding field was renamed to `failureKind` and dot
notation restored. No bracket-notation comparison remains anywhere in
`web/src` — verified — and the guard was left maximally strict rather than
narrowed to accommodate the collision.

**What is left is the gap itself.** The guard works for its named target and
silently does not for an equivalent spelling. Two shapes:

1. **Widen the pattern** to cover bracket notation and its quoting variants.
   Cheap, and worth pairing with a test asserting the guard *fails* on each
   spelling it claims to catch — a guard with no failing case is the same class
   of defect as a test that cannot go red.
2. **Narrow the guard's premise** so it matches conductor vocabulary rather than
   a bare field name, which is what produced the false positive in the first
   place and would remove the incentive to spell around it.

Low severity: no production behaviour depends on this, and the current tree is
clean. It is filed because a guard that reports coverage it does not have is a
standing invitation to the exact defect it exists to prevent, and because this
one has now demonstrably attracted an evasion once.

issues.body:
*Surface:* `deepseek-claude-headless` (and by extension any `*-claude-headless`
launcher) invoked from inside a Claude Code host session.

Two lanes were blocked by this today, at a point when Kimi was exhausted and
DeepSeek was the intended cheap fallback.

## Symptom

The launcher's read-only balance preflight succeeds, then the first model call
dies:

    Failed to authenticate. API Error: 401 Authentication Fails,
    Your api key: ****_wAA is invalid

## The error message is false, and the decisive evidence is that the key rotates

The configured key is fine. It returns HTTP 200 on the balance endpoint, on
`/anthropic/v1/messages` with `deepseek-v4-flash`, and on `/chat/completions`.

The masked value in the error **differs between runs** — `****WAAA` on one
launch, `****3QAA` on another. A rotating value is not a static API key; it is an
OAuth token being refreshed. So the child is not sending a corrupted DeepSeek
key, it is sending a *host Anthropic OAuth token* to DeepSeek's endpoint, which
correctly rejects it.

## Cause

The host session's OAuth-refresh selectors — `CLAUDE_CODE_SDK_HAS_HOST_AUTH_REFRESH`
and companions — leak into the child. The launcher unsets `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`,
`CLAUDE_API_KEY`, `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` and the provider keys, then exports
`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` from the key file, but the refresh selectors are not in
that unset list, and they take precedence at call time.

Clearing them with `env -u` fixes it; the same run then completes normally.

## Note the fix is not the opt-out the launcher advertises

The launcher also emits `⚠ Permission mode forced to default —
CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB is set`, which invites setting that variable to
`0`. **That is a different problem and the wrong lever here.** Both blocked lanes
declined to touch it, correctly: disabling a hardening measure so a credential
can flow is an environment change made to get past a block, which the repository
guidance rules out as a departure. The scrubber was never the cause — the leak is
inbound, not the key being stripped outbound.

An earlier coordinator hypothesis blamed the scrubber for stripping the child's
own auth. That was wrong, and the rotating masked value is what falsifies it.

## Suggested fix

Add the host OAuth-refresh selectors to the launcher's existing `unset` line, so
a child is isolated from the host session's credential refresh the same way it is
already isolated from static keys. Worth checking whether the sibling
`*-claude-headless` launchers share the omission, since the isolation block looks
common to them.

This is skillshare-governed global-skill territory, so it wants the `skillshare`
workflow rather than an in-place edit. Recorded here because it silently removes
a whole billing domain from the routing table at exactly the moment the
subscription pools are exhausted — which is when it is needed.
issues.title: Host OAuth-refresh selectors leak into headless children, so DeepSeek 401s with a rotating 'api key'

issues.body:
Severity: P3. Repository: cli-agent-orchestrator.

DEFECT. The local full-suite baseline is not stable, so "same failing set as
main" costs a re-run to establish instead of a comparison. Across six full runs
today on `feat/provider-controls-muse-agy-rows` and `main`, three distinct tests
failed intermittently and none reproduced on a second run of the same tree:

    test/services/test_fifo_reader.py::TestReaderThreadLifecycle::test_data_received_across_writer_reconnects
    test/cli/commands/test_install_opencode.py::TestOpencodeAgentListIntegration::test_installed_agent_visible_in_opencode_list
    test/security/test_auth.py::test_expected_audience_defaults_to_api_base_url_when_enabled
    test/security/test_auth.py::test_audience_fallback_enforced_in_validation

The two `test_auth` ids fail together in a full run and pass in isolation (39/39
on both trees), so they are order-dependent rather than timing-dependent. The
`fifo_reader` and `install_opencode` ids each appeared in exactly one run,
passed in isolation on both trees (31/31), and did not recur — thread and
subprocess timing.

SEPARATELY, three telemetry ids fail on every run for an environmental reason
rather than a defect:

    test/telemetry/test_otel_init.py::TestTelemetryEnabledExplicitly::test_enabled_installs_provider
    test/telemetry/test_otel_init.py::TestTelemetryEnabledExplicitly::test_double_init_does_not_replace_provider
    test/telemetry/test_otel_init.py::TestTelemetryEnabledExplicitly::test_shutdown_clears_module_handle

with `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=false but the OpenTelemetry SDK is not installed;
telemetry stays off. Install the extra: pip install cli-agent-orchestrator[otel]`.
These reproduce identically on clean `main`, so they are a venv-provisioning gap:
either the dev venv should install the `otel` extra, or the tests should skip
when the SDK is absent rather than fail.

WHY IT MATTERS. cond-0432 already records the hazard for a fixed baseline: "a
fifth failure appearing in the same run is easy to miss against four expected
ones." A baseline that also *moves* is worse, because the reviewer cannot tell a
new intermittent failure from a regression without re-running, and the honest
response to any surprise id becomes "run it again" rather than "investigate".
This nearly consumed a real review today: a sixth id appeared on a branch whose
change (deleting an unreachable argv binder) had no causal path to FIFO reader
threads, and establishing that took two full 8-minute runs plus isolation runs.

FIX DIRECTION, not prescribed. The telemetry three are the cheap half and should
be settled first, since they are deterministic and environmental. For the rest,
the useful artifact is a known-flaky list the suite itself can assert against, so
that an unexpected id is loud; marking them `xfail(strict=False)` would hide a
genuine regression in the same test and is worse than leaving them failing.
Order-dependence in `test_auth` is worth isolating directly — it reproduces
reliably in a full run, so it is diagnosable without hunting a race.

ACCEPTANCE. A full local run on clean `main` produces the same failing id set
twice in a row, and any deviation from that set is attributable without a re-run.

issues.body:
*Surface:* `conduct communication list`.

The command resolves the project for the **state directory**, then passes the
raw `args.project` as the **SQL filter**
(`conduct/commands/communication.py:117-124` into
`communication_store.list_communications(project_id=...)`).

With `--project` omitted and `CAO_TERMINAL_ID` set — the ordinary way a worker
invokes this — the state dir resolves correctly but `project_id` is `None`, so
the `WHERE project_id=?` clause matches nothing. The worker gets an **empty
list**, not a refusal.

## Why this is worse than a wrong filter

Empty and unfilterable are different answers, and the caller cannot tell them
apart. A worker asking for its own communications sees exactly what it would see
if its project genuinely had none, so the failure is silent and self-consistent.
Nothing in the output distinguishes "you asked about a project I could not
determine" from "that project has no communications".

This is the same class the `cond-0477` chain just closed at the catalog layer:
there, a required `task_occurrence_id` filter compared against an always-NULL
column and returned empty for every query. The lesson repeats — a filter built
from a value the command failed to resolve should refuse, naming what it could
not resolve, rather than silently returning the empty set that filter implies.

## Fix

Use the same resolved project for the filter that is used for the state
directory. If the project genuinely cannot be resolved, refuse with a typed
reason naming that, rather than querying with `None`.

Worth checking sibling commands for the same shape: a resolved value used for
one purpose and the raw argument used for another is easy to reproduce.

Found in passing by the PR 8 lane while verifying behavioural claims against
actual command behaviour, which is the practice that surfaced it — the guidance
being written would have described a command that does not do what it appears
to do.

Live file inspection (git log -S, grep) confirms defect absent. Vision: check now correctly scoped/closed; smallest check shipped. No further action. If re-observed, reopen with current file:line.
issues.title: conduct communication list filters on the raw --project, so a worker silently gets an empty list

issues.body:
*Surface:* `conduct/lib/workstate.py`, the projection layer.

Verified by the PR 8 lane: `workstate.py` imports neither `goal_store` nor
`coverage`. The projection has **no goal or hold awareness at all**, and its
`blocked` chip is documented as structurally unreachable — nothing can produce
it.

Two consequences, and they are separable.

## 1. A chip nothing writes

`blocked` is the projection-layer instance of the shape the composition audit
found nineteen times: a state named and rendered, with no writer. Per
`AGENTS.md`, delete what nothing writes, or ship its producer. Deleting is the
cheaper honest answer if goal/hold wiring is not coming soon; leaving it renders
a status the system can never report and quietly teaches a reader that "not
blocked" is a measured fact.

## 2. The projection cannot show what the semantic store now knows

PR 8 was assigned "typed reason/evidence/duration/release/resume detail views".
Those types now exist and are populated — `reason_kind`, `release_kind`,
`expectedness`, `decision_authority`, `resume_policy`, `deadline_at`, boundary
digests, and the `hold check` verdict with its reasons. The projection cannot
surface any of them, so an operator or supervisor reading workstate sees none of
the goal lifecycle this campaign built.

PR 8 shipped the **documentation** half — the typed vocabulary as the reference
a view renders — and deferred the wiring here deliberately, on two grounds:
`workstate.py` is a large file adjacent to live work, and the rendering surface
for a dashboard view is the fork, a different repository and a different failure
domain from skill text.

## One element is not buildable on honest terms, and should not be added later without solving this first

"Duration" in that bullet cannot mean elapsed time. The goal capsule explicitly
declines to emit wall/active/held time, with the recorded reason that there is no
honest source for it in this slice and **a zero would be indistinguishable from a
measured zero**. So a duration view today can only render `deadline_at`,
`created_at`, `recorded_at`, and `hold check --as-of` — points in time, not
intervals.

Anyone picking this up should treat elapsed-time duration as its own prerequisite
with its own honest source, not as a formatting exercise over existing columns.
Rendering a computed interval from timestamps that were never intended to measure
one would produce a number the system never established.

## Scope note

This is projection work, not semantic-store work. The store is correct and
populated; what is missing is a reader. Splitting it that way is deliberate:
whoever takes it should not need to touch `goal_store.py` or `coverage.py`.
issues.title: workstate projection has no goal/hold awareness, and its blocked chip is unreachable

issues.body:
An OpenCode-launched worker in the worktree cond0500-donor-revision built a
.git-common/ sandbox overlay (private refs/logs, objects symlinked to the real
store) and, during that setup, wrote into the SHARED .git of the real repository
/Users/colin/Projects/cli-agent-orchestrator instead of into its own overlay.

Two writes landed on the real repository:

1. .git/refs/heads/fix/cond0500-donor-revision was overwritten with the literal
   5 bytes "test\n" instead of a 40-hex OID (xxd: 7465 7374 0a). mtime 00:16.
2. .git/config gained core.bare = true on a clone that has a full working tree.
   mtime 23:32 the previous evening.

What I ran: git fetch origin --prune, from the fork during ordinary PR work.

What happened:
  fatal: bad object refs/heads/fix/cond0500-donor-revision
  error: ... did not send all necessary objects
and separately, git status in the primary checkout:
  fatal: this operation must be run in a work tree

What I expected: a normal fetch. Both failures are repository-wide, not
worktree-local: a broken ref aborts fetch for all ~40 attached worktrees, and
core.bare=true disables every worktree-aware command in the primary checkout.

Third effect, silent: with core.bare=true git stopped reconciling HEAD against
the files on disk, so the primary checkout desynced unnoticed - branch main
pointed at 1648f4a8 while the working tree held the tree of 62df9369.

No committed objects were lost. The true tip 691cd3a0 survived in the shared
object store and was recorded in TWO places: the worktree's per-worktree reflog
and the overlay's own refs/heads copy. The overlay had the correct value the
whole time; only the destination of the write was wrong.

Attribution, limited to what was established:
- CAO source contains no writer of .git-common. The only occurrence of the
  string is managed_provider_bridge.py:497, a read-only
  "git rev-parse --git-common-dir" used to build launch identity.
- The fork's own test suite has no .git-common fixture, no test writing a
  literal string into refs/heads/*, and no test setting core.bare.
So neither CAO nor its tests wrote these bytes. The overlay's "opencode" marker
file names the harness that did.

Repair applied and verified: git config --unset core.bare; ref restored to
691cd3a0; fetch succeeds; primary checkout fast-forwarded to origin/main after
confirming both stale states were ancestors of origin/main (so nothing unique
was discarded). Pre-repair .git/config preserved in the evidence directory. The
.git-common/ overlay was left in place untouched as evidence.

Why this is a CAO defect and not just cleanup: CAO launches these workers. A
worker sandbox able to write the shared .git of the operator's real repository
is the accidental-use-of-the-wrong-live-resource failure AGENTS.md names - a
good-faith sequence entering an illegal, repository-wide, silent state with no
actor positioned to notice it until an unrelated command failed.

Suggested guard, owned by the launch path that already has the information: the
launcher resolves --git-common-dir today for launch identity. It can compare
that resolved common dir against the sandbox root handed to the worker and
refuse the launch when a worker is about to treat the operator's shared .git as
its private overlay. That is a check on the launch tuple CAO already computes,
not a new ceremony, and its clearing verb is "point the worker at its own
overlay".
issues.title: an OpenCode worker sandbox overlay wrote into the shared .git, breaking fetch for every worktree

issues.body:
*Surface:* `conduct collect` (ordinary, non-retained) against a retained track
that is `active`.

Reproduced by execution during the cond-0484 lane. **This is present at base; it
is not introduced by that lane's change.**

## The sequence

A retained worker's track is `active` — for example because the worker cannot
produce the round report that parking requires (that is cond-0484). An operator
or supervisor runs ordinary `conduct collect`.

It returns **exit 0**. It deletes the terminal and releases the lease. And it
leaves `retained-track.json` at `active`, permanently.

Afterwards:

- `conduct retire` refuses: *already finalized as 'collected'*
- `conduct collect --retained` refuses: *retained track is 'active'*

## Why this is worse than either refusal alone

The two refusals are individually correct and contradict each other about the
same record — one reads the manifest, the other reads the track, and the
successful `collect` moved only the first. There is no verb that reconciles
them, so the record has no legal transition out for any actor.

The severity comes from the exit code. A refusal preserves the situation and
tells the caller something is wrong. **This reports success while destroying the
worker and stranding its record** — the pane is gone, the lease is released, and
the durable state now says two incompatible things. An operator following the
obvious path gets no signal at all until the next verb refuses, by which point
the terminal cannot be inspected because it no longer exists.

That ordering is the defect: the destructive half succeeded and the recording
half did not, and nothing recorded which leg failed.

## Relationship to cond-0484

cond-0484 is the trap that makes an `active` track common enough to meet this.
This issue is the sharper edge on it: the natural thing an operator reaches for
when a worker is stuck both looks like it worked and removes the evidence.

Fixing cond-0484 reduces how often this is encountered. It does not fix this,
because ordinary `collect` will still take this path on any `active` retained
track.

## Shape of a fix

Either ordinary `collect` recognises a retained track and refuses before
touching the terminal — naming `collect --retained` — or it performs both halves
so the track and the manifest cannot disagree. The first is smaller and is
probably right: a verb that is not the retained collector should decline the
retained case rather than half-perform it.

Whichever is chosen, the destructive step must not precede the recording step. A
partial failure should leave the worker alive and the record untouched, and
should say which leg failed.

issues.title: ordinary collect on an active retained track exits 0, tears down the worker, and strands the record

issues.body:
*Surface:* `tests/fake_cao.py`, the shared test double.

`FakeCao` answers `DELETE /terminals/<id>` with **200** but never removes the
terminal from its own dict. So any test that asserts terminal *presence* after a
delete is certifying nothing: the terminal is still there whether the code under
test issued the DELETE or not.

Found during the cond-0486 lane, as a near-miss. Its independent run appeared to
show the happy path returning exit 0 with the terminal still alive — a plausible
teardown defect. The lane chased it before believing it and found the fixture,
not the code. The assertion was corrected to the real observable (the DELETE on
the wire) and the trap documented in that test class.

## Why this needs fixing at source rather than in one test class

This is `AGENTS.md`'s named failure — **a fixture must model the thing, not the
expectation** — in a *shared* double. Every other test that checks presence after
a delete relies on the same nothing, and each one reads as a passing assertion
about teardown. The failure mode runs in both directions:

- a test asserting the terminal is **gone** after a delete can never pass, so
  nobody writes one, and teardown goes unpinned; and
- a test asserting the terminal is **still there** passes whether or not the
  code deleted it, so a real teardown regression stays green.

The second is the dangerous one, and it is invisible: the suite reports a
property it never checked.

## Fix

Make `DELETE` actually remove the terminal from the dict, so presence becomes a
real observable. Then audit existing call sites: some tests may be passing
*because* of the current behaviour, and those are the ones worth reading
closely — a test that goes red when the fixture starts modelling reality was
asserting the expectation.

Where a test genuinely wants to observe the request rather than the state,
asserting on the wire is the stronger check and should stay.

## Note for reviewers

A green result from a suite using this double is not evidence about teardown.
Two lanes in this campaign have independently mistaken fixture behaviour for
production behaviour — once here, and once where a Muse worker wrote its tests
against a hand-rolled stub client that mimicked the server, so the suite
certified the stub rather than the wiring.
issues.resolution: Triage 2026-08-21 vs vision + main 13bcdcc: Verified already-fixed on conductor main. Fix commit/proof cited in triage comment (see prior comment_id). Live file inspection (git log -S, grep) confirms defect absent. Vision: check now correctly scoped/closed; smallest check shipped. No further action. If re-observed, reopen with current file:line.
issues.title: FakeCao answers DELETE 200 without removing the terminal, so teardown assertions certify nothing

issues.body:
*Surface:* `muse-headless` under `--posture review` / `--posture edit` (its
sandbox is on in both); consequences land in `cao-conductor`'s test suite.

## The failure

Muse Code's headless sandbox blocks `socket.bind()` on loopback. In this
repository every test needing the in-process HTTP stub dies at
`tests/fake_cao.py` — `ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), _Handler)` raises
`PermissionError: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted`. Muse reported the same
failure for a bare `socket.bind(('127.0.0.1',0))` and attributed it to its
sandbox denying `require_escalated` under `--disable-approval`. That attribution
is unverified; what is established is that the bind fails in the child and
succeeds in the parent, so it is the sandbox and not the repository.

**`--posture yolo` disables the sandbox and is the operator-authorized route for
trusted local worktrees.** This issue records the trap for anyone who does not
use it.

## Why it is dangerous rather than merely annoying

It is **not a clean refusal.** The suite runs and reports
`Ran 70 tests … FAILED (errors=70)`. A worker that classifies this as
"environment-only, same at base" is technically correct and has verified nothing.

Blast radius: the fake server backs essentially every lifecycle test, so a
sandboxed worker can verify nothing touching spawn, report, collect, retire,
continue, park, track, or successor. What remains runnable is pure-logic modules
and AST/doc checks.

## The harm it actually caused

A worker's round-1 change shipped a **real race regression** — widening retire's
flock re-check let a retirement accept state an interleaved `conduct continue`
had just produced, breaking the pre-existing
`test_retire_track_cas_loses_to_same_generation_continue`.

It reported that round complete **with mutation evidence**. The evidence was a
bespoke `/tmp/verify_mutations.py` the worker wrote itself, which passed. The
real suite failed.

That is "a verification method that filters out its own signal" arriving through
the sandbox: unable to run the suite, the worker substituted a probe that could
only confirm what it already believed. A later round claimed "mutation-tested"
where the actual basis was "code review confirms each revert would make its test
RED" — a prediction reported as a measurement. Independently re-run, all six
reverts were genuinely red, which was partly luck: the round-1 claim had been
wrong.

## Mitigations that work

- **`--posture yolo`** for trusted local worktrees removes the cause.
- **Instruct the worker explicitly not to substitute a bespoke script**, and to
  say plainly what it could not run. This demonstrably works — once told, later
  rounds reported the block honestly instead of inventing evidence.
- **The lane manager runs every gate.** Muse writes, the manager verifies. That
  division is the cheapest reliable arrangement found.
- Never accept "mutation-tested" from a worker without the executed reverts.

## Two smaller traps in the same environment

- The worker could not write `.git/refs/heads/...` either, so it commits to a
  **detached HEAD and leaves the branch ref behind**. A caller that reads the
  branch ref to find the work concludes nothing was done. Two lanes hit ref-lock
  `EPERM`; one stopped and said so, one used `git commit-tree` plus a direct ref
  write.
- On a long round the final answer degenerated into a repeat loop, restating the
  same report five times. Substance was consistent, but anything parsing the tail
  of `final.txt` will misread it.
issues.title: Muse sandbox blocks loopback bind, so the suite errors rather than refuses and a worker can verify nothing

issues.body:
kimi-headless.sh backgrounds a wrapper subshell and records $! as 'pid' in
meta.json. kimi-headless-status.sh reads that .pid and decides liveness with
kill -0. That pid is the WRAPPER, not the agent: the agent is a separate
kimi-code process with an independent lifetime.

MEASURED, both workers against
/Users/colin/Projects/cao-conductor-worktrees/cond0486-report-on-behalf:

  reported pid 69463 -> gone;      actual agent 69469 ALIVE 20+ min, still editing
  reported pid 14674 -> exit 125;  actual agent 14682 ALIVE, still editing

Both agents confirmed in the worktree by 'lsof -a -p <pid> -d cwd'. Run 1 was
launched detached (nohup &) and its wrapper was reaped at a host command
boundary - a mode the skill documents. Run 2 was launched under harness process
management with --wait and its wrapper exited 125. BOTH paths orphaned a live
agent, so this is not specific to the detached mistake.

CONSEQUENCE. The caller believed both workers were dead. Both were alive in the
same worktree simultaneously:

- A test method (test_on_behalf_brings_retained_track_out_of_active) appeared in
  tests/test_report.py that neither the caller nor its saved copy contained.
- One agent ran a git operation that reverted the tree to clean, silently
  discarding ~500 lines of uncommitted work belonging to the other actor. It was
  recoverable only because copies had been saved aside for unrelated mutation
  testing.
- A full-suite differential was silently invalidated. Baseline: 1 pre-existing
  failure. 'Post-change': 7 failures naming 6 modules that read as regressions.
  Re-run under quiescent conditions after terminating both agents:
  tests.test_report 91 tests OK, none of the 6 reproduced. The runs were not
  equivalent, so the differential measured concurrency rather than the change.

That is the AGENTS.md rule: a differential is only as good as the equivalence of
its runs, and a measurement used as evidence must be taken under conditions the
report can state. Nothing in the launcher surface let the caller state those
conditions, because it reported both agents dead.

WHY THE DIRECTION MATTERS. Liveness is not merely unknown here; it is reported
confidently and wrongly, in the dangerous direction. 'Vanished' and 'finished'
both read to a caller as 'safe to reuse this workspace'. A caller that trusts
either will start a second worker on a directory a first is still writing -
which happened here twice. The same error inverted is the one this project
already names: a screen a detector does not recognise must never read as
completion.

REPAIR APPLIED. Terminated both orphaned agents by pid after confirming cwd. An
unrelated kimi-code in dnd-scheduler-worktrees (pid 30397) verified untouched
before and after. Work restored from saved copies and committed.

SUGGESTED FIX. Record the AGENT pid, not the wrapper's, and decide liveness from
it. The launcher already knows the agent process and the status helper already
has the right shape. Where the agent pid genuinely cannot be captured, report
liveness as UNKNOWN rather than resolving it from the wrapper: an unreadable
surface and an established absence are different answers, and only one of them
means the workspace is free.

Note this is the second instance today of one class - an uncoordinated actor
mutating a shared working resource the orchestrator believed it owned. cond-0509
is the first. If a third lands in this class, AGENTS.md's three-strikes rule
forces a written design review rather than another patch.
issues.resolution: Triage 2026-08-21 vs vision + main 13bcdcc: Verified already-fixed on conductor main. Fix commit/proof cited in triage comment (see prior comment_id). Live file inspection (git log -S, grep) confirms defect absent. Vision: check now correctly scoped/closed; smallest check shipped. No further action. If re-observed, reopen with current file:line.
issues.title: headless launcher reports liveness on the wrapper pid, so an orphaned agent keeps editing a workspace the caller believes is free

issues.body:
*Surface:* `conduct/lib/_retained.py`, `accepted_callback_report_for_round`, and
its callers `checkpoint --park`, `collect`, and now `retire`.

Two related defects, one specific and one general. The general one is the more
valuable finding.

## The specific defect: an untyped escape

`accepted_callback_report_for_round` reads
`report-identity-reconciliation.json` through a helper that catches only
`FileNotFoundError`. A **corrupt** reconciliation file therefore escapes as an
untyped exception rather than a typed refusal, breaking the
`{"ok": false, "error": {"failure_class": ...}}` contract every supervisor
parses. Confirmed by execution:

    UNTYPED JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 22 (char 21)

**Pre-existing and live on main today.** That block is byte-identical at
`d4150a5`, and `checkpoint --park` and `collect` already call this helper. The
cond-0484 change adds `retire` as a third caller inheriting it.

It does not record a falsehood — it fails loudly — so it is not urgent. But an
untyped traceback where a typed refusal is contracted is exactly what cond-0460
was filed for on a different surface.

## The general defect: one return value for two different observations

`accepted_callback_report_for_round` returns `None` for **both** "there is no
accepted report" and "I could not determine whether there is one", because it
swallows its own `AdmissionRefusal`.

This has now manufactured the same defect in a caller, and it is worth stating
plainly because it will do so again. In cond-0484 a seal was built to distinguish
three outcomes — accepted, absent, inconclusive — and its inconclusive branch was
**unreachable for the exact read failure it was written for**, because absent and
unreadable both arrived as `None`. The record then asserted "no accepted round
report exists for it", a negative nothing had established. That is the
`AGENTS.md` rule violated at one remove: *absent and unreadable are different
answers*, and *a refusal states what it observed, not what it assumed.*

The caller was repaired by reading the underlying store directly and
distinguishing the cases itself. That fix is correct and shipped, but it is a fix
in one caller. **A helper that collapses "nothing" and "couldn't look" will keep
manufacturing this defect in every caller that tries to be honest**, and each one
must independently rediscover that it cannot trust the helper's `None`.

## Why it was not fixed at the source

Deliberately out of scope for the cond-0484 P1 exit: the swallow is load-bearing
for `park` and `collect`'s canonical-path fallback, so changing it would alter
their admission behaviour. That is a real change to two working verbs, and it did
not belong inside an absorbing-state repair.

## Shape of the durable fix

Give the helper a return that can express three states rather than two — an
explicit inconclusive value, or a typed refusal the caller may catch — and then
migrate `park`, `collect` and `retire` onto it, checking at each site whether its
current fallback depends on `None` meaning "nothing". The migration is the work;
the signature change is small.

Doing so would also close the specific defect above, since the corrupt-file case
would then have somewhere honest to land.
issues.evidence: PR #221 merged b6d5d97; CallbackRecordAbsent typed distinction; mutation: revert hunks -> test_retained_callback_absent_type red (8 failures incl AdmissionRefusal escape), restore -> 9 OK; CI green exact head; post-merge suites OK
issues.title: accepted_callback_report_for_round returns None for both 'nothing' and 'could not look'

issues.body:
*Surface:* `tests/test_gc_workspaces.py::GcWorkspacesTest::test_collected_clean_run_reapable`.

This test fails deterministically on this machine at every SHA and passes in CI.
It has been carried as a standing exemption through **every lane of the
task/goal-lifecycle campaign** — briefs name it, receipts name it, and every gate
report subtracts it before declaring a clean run.

**There is no tracker issue for it.** Searched: nothing in `cao-system` names it.
Two issues have been cited for it in passing and neither covers it —
`cond-0506` is a `cli-agent-orchestrator` issue about *that* repository's
baseline instability, and `cond-0434` is about a load-flaky marshal session
cleanup test. So the exemption every gate depends on rests on nothing durable.

Verified just now on a clean checkout of current `origin/main` with no candidate
present: `Ran 10 tests` / `FAILED (failures=1)`. Deterministic, not a flake — it
fails on repetition, unlike the load-sensitive tests it gets grouped with.

## Why this is worth a record rather than a shrug

An exemption held only in prose decays exactly the way `AGENTS.md` describes.
Three concrete costs, all observed during this campaign:

- **It is repeatedly misattributed.** At least two different issue ids have been
  cited as its record, in briefs I wrote. A reader checking either finds
  something else and has to re-derive the exemption from scratch.
- **It masks its own neighbours.** Gate reports read "one failure, the documented
  exempt one" — so a *second* deterministic local failure appearing in the same
  file would be absorbed into the same sentence. The exemption is load-bearing
  for the claim "zero regressions" in a dozen receipts.
- **Nobody owns finding out why.** It is a real local/CI divergence in workspace
  reaping. Either the test depends on something CI has and this machine does not,
  or the reverse — and that difference has never been named, so it cannot be
  fixed or deliberately accepted.

## What would close it

Determine the divergence: what does the test assume about the workspace root,
filesystem, or environment that differs here. Then either fix the test so it
passes in both places, or mark it skipped-with-reason on the condition that
actually differs, so the suite reports a skip naming the cause instead of a
failure everyone has agreed to ignore.

A skip with a stated condition is honest and self-describing. A failure that
every reader is expected to know about is neither.
